questions.explanation: The phrase highlights that divine understanding encompasses wisdom’s origin, underlining that God alone fully comprehends wisdom (verse 23).

questions.text: What action does Job compare to searching for wisdom?
options: Looking in the depths of the sea
questions.explanation: Job describes the search for wisdom as a process of digging deep into the earth, emphasizing its hidden and precious nature (verses 1-11).

questions.text: Why does Job conclude that human effort cannot find wisdom?
options: It is only for the wise
questions.explanation: Job explains that wisdom is hidden from humans and cannot be acquired by search or effort, emphasizing its divine origin (verses 12-19).

questions.text: How does Job describe the relationship between wisdom and fearing God?
options: Fearing God is the beginning of wisdom
Wisdom is unrelated to fearing God
Fearing God is an outward act
questions.explanation: Job states that fearing the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, implying that reverence for God is the foundation of true understanding (verse 28:28).

questions.text: What is Job’s overall message about wisdom in Job 28?
options: It is more valuable than riches
It is only for the wise
questions.explanation: Job emphasizes that wisdom's worth surpasses material wealth and that it must be sought in reverence for God, highlighting its divine nature and value.

questions.text: In Job 29, what does Job recall about his past experiences?
options: He remembers his prosperity and respect he had.
He recalls his travels across nations.
He talks about building great cities.
questions.explanation: Job recalls his days when he was prosperous and honored, emphasizing the respect he once had (Job 29:2-3).

questions.text: What does Job say about how he contributed to the community in Job 29?
options: He delivered the poor and defended the orphans.
questions.explanation: Job describes himself as someone who helped the poor and the orphans, bringing justice to the afflicted (Job 29:12-13).

questions.text: According to Job 29, how did Job view his reputation among others?
questions.explanation: Job reflects on the honor and respect he enjoyed, noting his reputation as someone respected among people (Job 29:7-10).

questions.text: What aspect of Job’s appearance does he mention in Job 29?
questions.explanation: Job mentions how he adorned himself with robes and wore a crown of dignity, symbolizing his prosperity (Job 29:14).

questions.text: In Job 29, Job describes himself as walking in what manner?
questions.explanation: Job portrays walking in righteousness, justice, and integrity, as he reflects on his life (Job 29:14).

questions.text: How does Job describe his role related to the land and its people in Job 29?
options: He helped the humble and delivered the afflicted.
He built walls to defend the city.
questions.explanation: Job states that he was someone who helped the humble and the afflicted, showing his concern for justice (Job 29:12-13).

questions.text: What does Job express about his joy and blessing in Job 29?
options: He was filled with wealth and children.
His joy was in the prosperity and respect he had.
He enjoyed peace in his old age.
questions.explanation: Job reflects on his former joy, which was centered in his prosperity, respect, and the goodness he experienced, before his suffering (Job 29:2-3).

questions.text: What is a key theme of Job 29?
options: Remembrance of past blessings and integrity.
The importance of prayer and worship.
questions.explanation: Job reflects on his past blessings, blessings that included justice, respect, and righteousness, emphasizing his integrity during better days (Job 29).

questions.text: What does Job do in chapter 3 after his suffering begins?
options: He praises God for His goodness
He laments and curses the day of his birth
He offers sacrifices for his sins
questions.explanation: In Job 3, Job laments his suffering and curses the day of his birth, expressing deep despair (Job 3:1-10).

questions.text: How does Job express his feelings about his birth in this chapter?
options: He considers it a gift from God
He wishes he had never been born
He hopes to be reborn soon
questions.explanation: Job wishes he had never been born, saying he would have been at rest if he had died at birth (Job 3:11-13).

questions.text: What does Job say about the darkness in his grief?
options: It is a sign of spiritual darkness
It covers the faces of the day and night
questions.explanation: Job describes darkness covering the faces of the day and night, symbolizing his despair and hopelessness (Job 3:4-5).

questions.text: What is Job’s emotional state as he curses the day of his birth?
options: He is overwhelmed with grief and anger
questions.explanation: Job expresses intense grief and anger, wishing that his suffering had never begun and cursing the day (Job 3:11-12).

questions.text: According to Job 3, what does Job wish about the day he was born?
options: That it was never to be remembered
That it would be forgotten forever
questions.explanation: Job wishes the day of his birth was never seen, expressing a desire that it had not come into existence (Job 3:3).

questions.text: What does Job declare about his suffering in this chapter?
options: He accepts it as God's will
He believes it will end soon
He wishes death would come quickly
He sees it as a test of faith
questions.explanation: Job expresses a desire for death, wishing that the darkness and misery would end (Job 3:23), indicating his wish for relief from suffering.

questions.text: How does Job’s opening of chapter 3 set the tone for his speech?
options: It begins with praise and thanksgiving
It starts with intense lament and complaint
It opens with a prayer for himself
questions.explanation: Job's speech begins with a profound lament, cursing the day of his birth and voicing his despair (Job 3:1-10), setting a tone of deep sorrow.

questions.text: Which theme is most prominent in Job chapter 3?
questions.explanation: The chapter primarily focuses on Job expressing his grief and despair, wishing he had never been born as a result of his suffering (Job 3).

questions.text: In Job 30, who are described as mocking Job?
questions.explanation: Job describes the men as 'despicable men' who scorn him (Job 30:1), highlighting their contempt.

questions.text: What have Job's tormentors replaced his friends with?
questions.explanation: Job mentions that his tormentors are like young vultures that scavenge and mock him (Job 30:27).

questions.text: According to Job 30, how do Job's friends' actions contrast with his suffering?
questions.explanation: Job describes that his friends' actions include mocking him and scorning him (Job 30:9-10).

questions.text: What does Job say about the continuation of his suffering?
options: It is continuing worse every day
It is a test from God
questions.explanation: Job laments that his suffering continues and worsens, emphasizing ongoing distress (Job 30:15).

questions.text: How does Job describe the laughter of his friends in Job 30?
questions.explanation: Job indicates that his friends’ laughter is filled with mockery, not genuine joy (Job 30:10).

questions.text: What physical state does Job compare his suffering to in Job 30?
questions.explanation: Job depicts his suffering as unbearable, similar to a garment that is being stretched and torn (Job 30:18).

questions.text: Who does Job say has become his mockers in Job 30?
questions.explanation: Job refers to young men who mock him, highlighting the contempt he faces (Job 30:1).

questions.text: According to Job 30, what is Job’s attitude toward his own suffering?
options: He laments that he is ignored
questions.explanation: Job expresses despair and questions why he is forsaken or ignored amid his suffering (Job 30:20).

questions.text: In Job 31, what does Job declare he made a pact with regarding his eyes?
options: Not to gaze lustfully at a young woman
Not to look upon a foreign land
Not to observe the rich and powerful
questions.explanation: Job 31:1 states that Job made a covenant with his eyes not to look lustfully at a young woman, demonstrating his commitment to purity and integrity.

questions.text: What describes Job’s attitude toward favoring the wicked in Job 31?
options: He admits to secretly favoring them
questions.explanation: In Job 31:7-8, Job states he did not walk with falsehood or favor the wicked, emphasizing his integrity before God.

questions.text: Which sin does Job explicitly say he avoided in Job 31?
questions.explanation: Job 31:13-14 mentions Job’s concern about being judged by God if he despised the cause of his servant or maid, implying avoidance of malicious winking or disrespect.

questions.text: How does Job describe his treatment of the poor and needy?
options: He rescued them and extended his hand to the poor
questions.explanation: Job 31:16-22 describes how Job did not deny the needs of the poor and needy, and he actively helped them by providing clothing and sustenance.

questions.text: What does Job say about his honesty in dealing with his workers in Job 31?
options: He exploited them for personal gain
He upheld fairness and did not oppress them
questions.explanation: In Job 31:13-15, Job affirms that he treated his servants justly and with integrity, recognizing that they are God’s servants too.

questions.text: What does Job declare would happen if he had denied justice to others?
options: He would be acknowledged for his efforts
God would hear and punish him
questions.explanation: Job 31:14 states that if Job had denied justice, God would arise to judge him, highlighting the importance of integrity before God.

questions.text: What does Job say about his actions towards those who owed him money or services?
options: He refused to lend or lend out his property
He kept his wealth to himself
He did not oppress or take ransom for his servants' release
questions.explanation: In Job 31:16-23, Job emphasizes that he did not keep back the poor or oppress his servants, nor did he take ransom for their release, demonstrating his fairness.

questions.text: What overarching theme does Job emphasize throughout Job 31?
options: His unwavering integrity and righteousness before God
His desire for revenge against enemies
questions.explanation: Throughout Job 31, Job consistently affirms his innocence, integrity, and adherence to righteousness before God, reflecting his desire to live rightly.

questions.text: What is the main reason Elihu begins to speak in Job 32?
options: He feels compelled to speak because others have been silent
questions.explanation: Elihu states that he feels compelled because Job and the others have spoken but not correctly, and he feels the need to respond (Job 32:1-4).

questions.text: Who does Elihu say he was waiting to speak until they finished?
questions.explanation: Elihu mentions he held back because the others were older, and he wanted to listen until they finished speaking (Job 32:4).

questions.text: What does Elihu say about God's justice in Job 32?
options: God does no wrong or partiality
questions.explanation: Elihu emphasizes that God does no wrong or partiality, highlighting God's justice (Job 32:10, 12).

questions.text: How does Elihu describe the way he speaks in Job 32?
options: He speaks with restraint and caution
He speaks merely to follow tradition
questions.explanation: Elihu states that he speaks with restraint and does not rush into words, aiming for careful speech (Job 32:18-19).

questions.text: Which metaphor does Elihu use to describe his words in Job 32?
questions.explanation: Elihu compares his words to a shout that bursts within him, indicating intense feeling (Job 32:18).

questions.text: What qualities does Elihu highlight about himself in Job 32?
options: He is young and eager for understanding
questions.explanation: Elihu describes himself as young but eager and full of words, seeking understanding (Job 32:6-7).

questions.text: What does Elihu say he will do if he finds words that are right?
questions.explanation: Elihu indicates he will speak what is right if he finds words that are correct (Job 32:4).

questions.text: Which aspect of Job's friends' speeches prompts Elihu to speak?
questions.explanation: Elihu feels compelled to speak because the friends have justified God's justice but have not adequately addressed Job's concerns, and he seeks to add understanding (Job 32:9, 12).

questions.text: In Job 33, Elihu begins by urging Job to do what?
questions.explanation: Elihu encourages Job to listen carefully to what he is about to say (Job 33:1-2).

questions.text: According to Elihu in Job 33, what might God do if He finds sin in a person?
questions.explanation: Elihu states that if God finds sin, He rebukes a person with pain to turn them from their iniquity (Job 33:19-24).

questions.text: What is one reason Elihu gives for God allowing suffering?
questions.explanation: Elihu suggests that suffering can be a form of God's discipline aimed at correction (Job 33:16-18).

questions.text: What does Elihu say about God's speaking to humans?
options: God communicates in dreams and pain
questions.explanation: Elihu mentions that God may speak to people through dreams and suffering to guide or correct them (Job 33:14-16).

questions.text: What is Elihu's view of wise men’s ability to discern God's messages?
questions.explanation: Elihu emphasizes that wisdom comes from God and that understanding divine messages requires divine insight (Job 33:33).

questions.text: What does Elihu suggest about refusing correction?
questions.explanation: Elihu implies that refusing correction can result in spiritual ruin, as correction is beneficial for growth (Job 33:27-28).

questions.text: What role does Elihu assign to suffering in God's process?
questions.explanation: Elihu views suffering as part of God's training process to teach or correct the individual (Job 33:19-23).

questions.text: What is Elihu’s overall message regarding God's dealings with humans?
questions.explanation: Elihu emphasizes that God's discipline is just and aimed at bringing people back to righteousness (Job 33:26-27).

questions.text: What is Elihu doing in Job 34?
options: He is speaking to critique Job
questions.explanation: Elihu begins to speak to Job, criticizing him and offering his perspective (Job 34:1-4).

questions.text: According to Elihu, who is responsible for all God's acts?
questions.explanation: Elihu emphasizes that God is responsible for all His acts and deeds (Job 34:10).

questions.text: What does Elihu say about God’s justice in Job 34?
questions.explanation: Elihu states that God does no wrong and is just in all His ways (Job 34:12).

questions.text: How does Elihu describe God's oversight of the earth?
options: He leaves it to natural laws
questions.explanation: Elihu states that God controls and upholds the earth, overseeing all that happens (Job 34:13-14).

questions.text: What does Elihu say about God's power over life and death?
questions.explanation: Elihu emphasizes that God has sovereign power over life and death (Job 34:14-15).

questions.text: What assertion does Elihu make about God's responses to humans' deeds?
questions.explanation: Elihu asserts that God judges righteously, without partiality (Job 34:17).

questions.text: What warning does Elihu give to Job in Job 34?
options: To trust in his own wisdom
questions.explanation: Elihu calls Job to recognize God's righteousness and accept His justice (Job 34:33).

questions.text: In Job 34, Elihu emphasizes which of the following about God's actions?
options: God acts according to human wishes
God is unaware of human suffering
God is limited by human sin
questions.explanation: Elihu underscores that God's ways are just, and He does not act unjustly (Job 34:12-15).

questions.text: According to Job 35, what does Elihu imply about God's justice?
options: God always responds to a person's plea
God's justice is sometimes beyond human understanding
God does not care about human suffering
God is quick to punish the wicked
questions.explanation: Elihu suggests that God's justice may be beyond human perception, especially when he mentions that God's ways are often inscrutable (Job 35:10-13).

questions.text: What does Elihu say about human complaints in Job 35?
options: They are always justified before God
They do not make God listen any more than lightning calls to heaven
questions.explanation: Elihu compares human complaints to lightning calling from heaven, implying that mere complaints do not influence God's response (Job 35:15).

questions.text: What does Elihu say about God's concern for innocent suffering in Job 35?
options: God punishes the innocent as well as the guilty
God is indifferent to human suffering
God does not concern Himself with the righteous
God considers the suffering of the innocent but remains just
questions.explanation: Elihu emphasizes that God is just and does not ignore innocent suffering, suggesting that He values righteousness (Job 35:12-13).

questions.text: Why does Elihu believe that Job’s complaints are insignificant in Job 35?
options: Because Job has no faith in God
Because complaints do not influence God's greatness
Because God's justice is already established
questions.explanation: Elihu states that human complaints are insignificant compared to God's greatness and majesty (Job 35:14-15).

questions.text: What is Elihu’s attitude towards God's silence when humans cry out to Him?
options: He believes God is ignoring their cries
He recognizes that God's silence is part of His divine justice
He thinks God is angry and withholds His response
He suggests humans should stop crying out
questions.explanation: Elihu implies that God's silence does not mean indifference, but is part of His divine justice and plan (Job 35:15).

questions.text: According to Job 35, what does Elihu say about God's power?
options: God's power is limited by human sin
God’s power is infinite and unmatched
God’s power is only for the righteous
God’s power can easily be challenged by humans
questions.explanation: Elihu emphasizes the infinite and unmatched nature of God's power, which is beyond human challenge (Job 35:10-11).

questions.text: What does Elihu suggest about the reason why God might delay in responding?
options: To teach people patience and humility
Because God has no interest in Job's situation
To punish those who oppose Him
questions.explanation: Elihu indicates that God's delays serve to teach patience, humility, and His divine purposes (Job 35:14-16).

questions.text: What is Elihu’s conclusion about human influence on God's actions in Job 35?
options: Humans can influence God's decisions through prayer
Humans have no power to influence God's justice
God changes His mind based on human pleas
Humans can plead to delay or stop God's judgments
questions.explanation: Elihu concludes that humans do not have the power to influence God's justice or decisions (Job 35:16).

questions.text: What does Elihu say about God's greatness in Job 36?
options: God does not care for humans
questions.explanation: Elihu emphasizes that God's deeds are beyond human comprehension, highlighting His greatness (Job 36:26).

questions.text: According to Elihu, what should people do in response to God's greatness?
options: Fear and serve Him with reverence
questions.explanation: Elihu calls on humans to fear and serve God humbly, acknowledging His justice and greatness (Job 36:14-15).

questions.text: What does Elihu say about God's treatment of the afflicted?
questions.explanation: Elihu states that God is compassionate and delivers the afflicted from suffering (Job 36:15).

questions.text: Which characteristic of God does Elihu highlight regarding His justice?
options: He is slow to anger and great in power
questions.explanation: Elihu describes God's justice as balanced with patience and power, emphasizing His greatness (Job 36:5, 11).

questions.text: What does Elihu warn will happen if people ignore God’s correction?
questions.explanation: Elihu indicates that ignoring God's correction can lead to destruction or downfall (Job 36:18-19).

questions.text: How does Elihu describe the purpose of God's discipline?
questions.explanation: Elihu states that God's discipline is meant to turn people from evil and lead them to righteousness (Job 36:10, 12).

questions.text: What does Elihu say about the silence of mankind in relation to God's works?
options: People often remain silent and ignore Him
People speaks frequently about His justice
questions.explanation: Elihu remarks that people fail to see or understand God's works because of their silence or blindness (Job 36:21).

questions.text: What attitude does Elihu encourage toward God's correction?
questions.explanation: Elihu encourages humility and submission to God's discipline, recognizing His justice and greatness (Job 36:10-12).

questions.text: What natural phenomenon is described in Job 37 as part of God's mighty works?
questions.explanation: Job 37 describes lightning and snow as part of God's mighty displays of power (verses 3-5).

questions.text: According to Job 37, how does God speak during storms?
questions.explanation: The chapter emphasizes that God speaks through thunder, illustrating His power (verse 2).

questions.text: What is Job’s response to the storm and God's power as described in this chapter?
questions.explanation: Job expresses reverence and awe, acknowledging God's greatness (verses 14-16).

questions.text: What does Job 37 say about the direction of God's voice during storms?
options: It is heard from one part of the sky to another
It only occurs during the day
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that God's voice can be heard across the sky, from one end to the other (verse 4).

questions.text: In Job 37, what does the text suggest about God's control over creation's storms?
options: They are deliberately commanded by God
They happen only during specific seasons
They are caused by celestial bodies
questions.explanation: The passage indicates that storms are under God's command, showcasing His sovereignty over nature (verses 2-5).

questions.text: What does Job 37 imply about the purpose of God's storm displays?
options: To display His power and glory
questions.explanation: The chapter highlights that divine storms reveal God's mighty power and glory (verses 5-13).

questions.text: How does Job describe the beauty of God's creation in this chapter?
questions.explanation: Job emphasizes the majestic and awe-inspiring aspects of God's creation, especially storms and natural phenomena (verses 10-13).

questions.text: What attitude does Job encourage in response to God's mighty works as seen in Job 37?
questions.explanation: Job encourages reverence and awe, recognizing God's power in creation and His sovereignty (verses 14-16).

questions.text: In Job 38, God begins speaking out of a whirlwind. What question does He ask Job first?
options: Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?
Who marked off the dimensions of the sea?
Can you count the stars in the sky?
Do you know the way to the land of Uz?
questions.explanation: God's first question to Job in Job 38 asks, 'Where were you when I laid the Earth's foundations?' (Job 38:4), emphasizing God's role as Creator and Job's limited understanding.

questions.text: Which of the following does God describe as having set its boundaries in Job 38?
questions.explanation: God references setting boundaries for the sea, saying He told it where its waves should stop (Job 38:8-11), demonstrating His control over nature.

questions.text: What question does God ask Job about the dawn in Job 38?
options: Have you commanded the morning since your days began?
Can you bring forth the dawn at your command?
Do you know where the sun rises?
Has the dawn ever forsaken the earth?
questions.explanation: God asks Job if he has commanded the morning or shown the dawn its place (Job 38:12-13), highlighting God's sovereignty over the day and night.

questions.text: According to Job 38, what does God ask Job about the channels of the sea?
options: Who closed the doors when it burst forth?
Can you hold back the water?
questions.explanation: God questions Job about who closed the sea's doors when it burst out from the depths (Job 38:8), emphasizing God's power in controlling the sea's boundaries.

questions.text: In Job 38, God challenges Job to do which of the following regarding the weather?
options: Call for rain whenever you want
Command the clouds to pour rain
Set the boundaries for the clouds
questions.explanation: God asks if Job can set the clouds in their bounds (Job 38:9), demonstrating His authority over weather patterns.

questions.text: What is one theme emphasized in Job 38?
questions.explanation: A central theme of Job 38 is God's sovereignty and control over creation, as He questions Job about the natural order and His divine authority.

questions.text: How does God describe His knowledge of the earth in Job 38?
options: He formed the earth and knows its dimensions
He created the land with his hands
He is the maker and sustainer
questions.explanation: God mentions that He laid the earth’s foundation and understands its measurements (Job 38:4-6), indicating His detailed knowledge of creation.

questions.text: What is Job’s response to God's speeches in Job 38?
options: He humbly admits he is unworthy
questions.explanation: Job responds with silence and acknowledges God's wisdom, humbly listening to God's words in Job 38 (Job 38:1-3).

questions.text: What animal's strength does God describe as powerful in Job 39?
questions.explanation: In Job 39:19-25, God describes the lion as a mighty creature with great strength. The lion’s roar and hunting prowess exemplify strength and power.

questions.text: According to Job 39, what does the wild goat do that demonstrates independence?
questions.explanation: Job 39:1-3 describes the wild goat as free, able to climb mountaintops and leap over rocks, symbolizing independence and agility.

questions.text: How does Job 39 describe the ostrich’s behavior regarding its eggs?
options: Puts eggs in nests on the ground
questions.explanation: Job 39:13-15 mentions the ostrich laying eggs on the ground and neglecting to shut them, trusting the earth to keep them safe, highlighting a distinctive behavior.

questions.text: What does God say about the horse in Job 39?
questions.explanation: In Job 39:19-25, God states that the horse is created for battle, describing its strength and readiness for war.

questions.text: What is the primary theme of Job 39?
questions.explanation: The chapter focuses on God's creation of various animals and His sovereignty over nature, illustrating His power and wisdom in creation.

questions.text: What does Job 39 imply about God's knowledge of wild animals?
options: He is unaware of their habits
He created and understands each one
He concerns Himself only with humans
questions.explanation: Throughout Job 39, God describes animals’ behaviors as part of His creation, showing His understanding of each species’ nature.

questions.text: Which animal is described as being able to 'stand unshaken in the field' in Job 39?
questions.explanation: Job 39:13-15 describes the ostrich as trembling not, even in open fields, highlighting its resilience.

questions.text: In Job 39, which characteristic of the horse is highlighted by God?
options: Its ability to run long distances
questions.explanation: God emphasizes the horse’s readiness for warfare, describing its loud snorting and fierceness in Job 39:21.

questions.text: Who does Eliphaz accuse Job of being like in Job 4:7-8?
questions.explanation: Eliphaz suggests that Job's suffering is a result of his own actions, similar to those who plant evil and reap trouble (Job 4:7-8).

questions.text: What does Eliphaz say about the quickness of man’s downfall in Job 4:8?
questions.explanation: Eliphaz states that those who sow trouble will reap it quickly, implying that downfall follows actions promptly (Job 4:8).

questions.text: In Job 4, what does Eliphaz claim about those who are innocent?
options: They are not attacked by disaster
questions.explanation: Eliphaz implies that innocent people are not those who are destroyed or face calamities prematurely (Job 4:7-8).

questions.text: What modern concept is reflected in Eliphaz's statement about reaping what one sows?
questions.explanation: Eliphaz's words echo the idea of retributive justice—that actions have corresponding consequences, a concept similar to karma and biblical reaping (Job 4:8).

questions.text: How does Eliphaz describe the appearance of God's angel in Job 4:18?
questions.explanation: Eliphaz describes God's angel as ‘perfect in wisdom’, emphasizing divine perfection (Job 4:18).

questions.text: What is Eliphaz's view on God's trustworthiness toward his angels in Job 4:18?
questions.explanation: Eliphaz indicates that God trusts His angels completely, describing their perfection in wisdom (Job 4:18).

questions.text: According to Eliphaz in Job 4:17, what question is posed about humans?
options: Are humans more righteous than God?
questions.explanation: Eliphaz questions whether a human is more righteous or pure than God, implying God's supreme justice (Job 4:17).

questions.text: What overall theme does Job 4 primarily address?
questions.explanation: The chapter deals with the perceived justice of God and the idea that humans should not question God's fairness, as reflected in Eliphaz's speeches (Job 4).

questions.text: What challenge does God issue to Job in Job 40:2?
options: To answer Him if he can
questions.explanation: God challenges Job to answer Him and justify himself, highlighting Job's accusations (Job 40:2).

questions.text: Which creature does God describe as 'a great and mighty beast' in Job 40?
questions.explanation: God refers to Behemoth as 'a great and mighty beast,' emphasizing His own power in creation (Job 40:15).

questions.text: According to Job 40, what is said about the strength of Behemoth?
options: He is swift like the wind
He is the foremost of God's creations
He dwells in the depths of the sea
questions.explanation: God describes Behemoth as 'the foremost of God's works,' reflecting its strength and significance (Job 40:19).

questions.text: What command does God give Job regarding Behemoth in Job 40?
questions.explanation: God asks Job to behold Behemoth and consider its ways, emphasizing God's creative power (Job 40:19).

questions.text: In Job 40, God's tone can be described as:
questions.explanation: God's tone is commanding and assertive as He confronts Job, emphasizing His authority (Job 40:1-2).

questions.text: How does Job respond to God's challenge in Job 40?
options: He admits his ignorance and cannot answer
questions.explanation: Job acknowledges his limitations and says he cannot answer God's questions, recognizing God's sovereignty (Job 40:3-5).

questions.text: What is the primary theme emphasized in Job 40?
options: God's sovereignty and power in creation
questions.explanation: The chapter emphasizes God's sovereignty and control over creation, demonstrated through His description of Behemoth (Job 40:8-19).

questions.text: What does God's description of Behemoth teach about His creative power?
options: He creates beings that are mighty and fearless
He creates beings to serve humans
He creates creatures that live in the sea
questions.explanation: God describes Behemoth as a mighty creature to illustrate His incredible power in creating strong and fearless beings (Job 40:15-19).

questions.text: What creature is described as unstoppable and formidable in Job 41?
questions.explanation: Job 41 describes Leviathan as an unstoppable and mighty creature, emphasizing its strength and resilience (Job 41:1-34).

questions.text: According to Job 41, what is one way Leviathan's strength is characterized?
questions.explanation: Job 41 describes Leviathan as having a thick, impenetrable armor, making it nearly invincible (Job 41:15-17).

questions.text: What is the Leviathan described as doing when disturbed?
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that Leviathan trembles and causes chaos when disturbed (Job 41:29-30).

questions.text: In Job 41, what is implied about Leviathan’s power over humans?
options: Humans are afraid but can kill it
questions.explanation: The text emphasizes that only God can tame Leviathan, highlighting its divine origin and power (Job 41:1-10).

questions.text: What does Job 41 suggest about Leviathan's role in creation?
options: An awe-inspiring part of God's creation
questions.explanation: The chapter presents Leviathan as a creature fully part of God's creation, emphasizing God's sovereignty over it (Job 41:11-25).

questions.text: How does Job respond to God’s description of Leviathan in Job 41?
options: He admits his inability to confront it
He claims to have tamed it
questions.explanation: Job acknowledges that only God can control Leviathan, implying human limitations and God's supreme power (Job 41:10).

questions.text: What is one of the sensory features of Leviathan described in Job 41?
questions.explanation: Job 41 mentions Leviathan's fearsome teeth as part of its formidable appearance (Job 41:14).

questions.text: What overarching lesson about God's power can be drawn from Job 41?
options: God's sovereignty over the natural world
questions.explanation: The chapter underscores God's sovereignty and power over even the most formidable creatures like Leviathan, reminding us of God's supreme authority (Job 41:11, 34).

questions.text: Who responds to Job at the end of Job 42, expressing God's greatness?
questions.explanation: Elihu is the one who speaks to Job and then responds to God's speech in Job 42:7-8, emphasizing God's greatness and justice.

questions.text: What does Job do after God's speeches conclude?
questions.explanation: Job repents in dust and ashes after God's speeches, acknowledging God's sovereignty (Job 42:6).

questions.text: What does Job receive at the end of the chapter that signifies restoration?
questions.explanation: God restores Job’s fortunes, giving him twice as much as before (Job 42:10).

questions.text: How does God describe Job in His speech in Job 42?
questions.explanation: God affirms that Job is a righteous man, distinguished from others by his integrity (Job 42:7).

questions.text: What is the main theme of Job’s response in Job 42:1-6?
questions.explanation: Job admits God's sovereignty and his own limited understanding, expressing trust and humility (Job 42:2-6).

questions.text: What does Job's fortune symbolize after his restoration?
questions.explanation: The restored possessions symbolize God's blessing and Job's renewed prosperity (Job 42:10).

questions.text: What was Job's initial reaction to God's speeches in Job 42?
questions.explanation: Job responds with repentance in dust and ashes, acknowledging God's sovereignty (Job 42:6).

questions.text: How many sons and daughters does Job have after his restoration?
questions.explanation: Job's new family includes seven sons and three daughters, as stated in Job 42:13-15.

questions.text: What does Eliphaz call Job to do in Job 5:1?
questions.explanation: Eliphaz encourages Job to call his friends or wise men for help, suggesting they may provide guidance (Job 5:1).

questions.text: According to Job 5:2, what can anger cause?
questions.explanation: Eliphaz states that anger causes destruction, highlighting its destructive power (Job 5:2).

questions.text: What does Eliphaz say about divine help in Job 5:8?
options: It is for those who seek God
questions.explanation: Eliphaz emphasizes that seeking God is the way to find help from divine power (Job 5:8).

questions.text: What does Job 5:15 say about divine rescue?
questions.explanation: Eliphaz assures that God delivers those who are in trouble, rescuing the needy (Job 5:15).

questions.text: In Job 5:16, what is the result of God’s intervention?
questions.explanation: Eliphaz suggests that God's intervention helps the weak and alleviates their hardship (Job 5:16).

questions.text: According to Job 5:17, how should one regard God's discipline?
questions.explanation: Eliphaz indicates that God's discipline is for correction and benefit, not punishment alone (Job 5:17).

questions.text: What does Eliphaz imply about the joy of the innocent in Job 5:18?
questions.explanation: He says that God wounds but also binds up, implying suffering may be part of divine discipline (Job 5:18).

questions.text: What does Eliphaz encourage Job to do in Job 5:27?
questions.explanation: Eliphaz advises Job to observe the patterns of life and seek wisdom, indicating God's ways are known through understanding (Job 5:27).

questions.text: What does Job compare his suffering to in Job 6:2?
options: A burden too heavy to bear
questions.explanation: Job describes his anguish as weighing heavily, saying it weighs 'like scales' on him, emphasizing the severity of his distress (Job 6:2-3).

questions.text: How does Job describe his words in Job 6:3?
questions.explanation: Job states his words are 'bitter' and 'accursed' because of his suffering, reflecting his feelings of despair (Job 6:3).

questions.text: What does Job say about his friends in Job 6:14?
options: They seek to help him spiritually
questions.explanation: Job laments that anyone who would truly pity him and seek his well-being is treating him as if he were a stranger or enemy (Job 6:14).

questions.text: According to Job 6:10, what does Job feel about losing hope?
options: He is uncertain about his future
questions.explanation: Job expresses a desire that even if he is rebuked, he would not be part of the pain, indicating his overwhelming despair (Job 6:9-10).

questions.text: What does Job say about his friends’ responses in Job 6:24?
questions.explanation: Job asks his friends to show him where he has gone wrong, implying they have accused him unjustly (Job 6:24).

questions.text: What does Job request from his friends in Job 6:27?
questions.explanation: Job asks his friends to consider whether they are justified in their accusations against him, urging them to reflect on his words (Job 6:27).

questions.text: What is one of Job’s main complaints in Job 6:5?
options: That he has been unjustly accused
That his suffering is too great
questions.explanation: Job states that his suffering, like a wild donkey or a wild ox, is loud and persistent, indicating the severity and noise of his pain (Job 6:5).

questions.text: How does Job feel about the possibility of comfort from his friends in Job 6:14?
options: They should help him rather than run away
They should rebuke him more sharply
questions.explanation: Job urges his friends to be willing to help and not to treat him as a stranger, showing his desire for genuine comfort (Job 6:14).

questions.text: What does Job compare life to in Job 7:1?
questions.explanation: Job describes life as a hired man’s toil and labor, emphasizing its temporary and tiring nature (Job 7:1).

questions.text: According to Job 7:3, what has Job’s suffering been compared to?
questions.explanation: Job mentions his time as being like restless nights that bring no relief (Job 7:3).

questions.text: In Job 7:5, what does Job say about his flesh?
questions.explanation: Job describes his flesh as being full of worms and wasting away (Job 7:5).

questions.text: What does Job pray for in Job 7:17-18?
options: To be hidden from God’s fury
To be watched over by God
questions.explanation: Job asks God why He pays attention to humans and observes them (Job 7:17-18), reflecting his desire for divine awareness and concern.

questions.text: How does Job describe his life in Job 7:16?
questions.explanation: Job states that he wishes he could vanish and have no more life (Job 7:16).

questions.text: What does Job say about the length of his days in Job 7:1-2?
questions.explanation: Job describes his days as fleeting and burdensome, like a hired man's long labor (Job 7:1-2).

questions.text: What imagery does Job use to describe his suffering in Job 7:5?
questions.explanation: Job explicitly mentions worms and wasting away as part of his suffering (Job 7:5).

questions.text: In Job 7:20, what does Job ask God to do?
questions.explanation: Job asks God to hide His face from his sins and not consider iniquity (Job 7:20), showing his plea for divine mercy and not to be scrutinized.

questions.text: Who begins to speak in Job 8?
questions.explanation: Eliphaz is the one who speaks at the start of Job 8, urging Job to consider God's justice (Job 8:1-3).

questions.text: What does Eliphaz suggest about God's justice in Job 8?
options: God does not see human actions
questions.explanation: Eliphaz implies that God will not pervert justice or condemn the innocent unjustly (Job 8:3-4).

questions.text: What is suggested about the fate of the wicked in Job 8?
options: They will repent and be forgiven
questions.explanation: Eliphaz asserts that wicked people will be cut off, indicating divine judgment (Job 8:6-7).

questions.text: What does Eliphaz say about prosperity after hardship in Job 8?
questions.explanation: He suggests that prosperity will come again after trouble, like a plant pushing through the earth (Job 8:16-17).

questions.text: What does Eliphaz imply about God's ability to destroy the wicked?
questions.explanation: Eliphaz emphasizes God's power to destroy the wicked and uphold justice, implying God's reliability (Job 8:3).

questions.text: According to Job 8, how should one respond to God's justice?
questions.explanation: Eliphaz encourages Job to consider God's justice and to humble himself before God (implied through his reasoning).

questions.text: What natural analogy does Eliphaz use to describe prosperity in Job 8?
questions.explanation: Eliphaz compares prosperity to a plant or root emerging from the earth, symbolizing renewal and growth (Job 8:16).

questions.text: What overall theme does Job 8 convey about God's justice?
questions.explanation: Eliphaz emphasizes that God judges justly, punishing the wicked and supporting the innocent, encouraging Job to trust God's justice (Job 8:3-4).

questions.text: In Job 9, who is described as unable to be contended with?
questions.explanation: Job 9 describes God as the one who is 'exalted in power' and whom no one can challenge or contend with (Job 9:4-8).

questions.text: According to Job 9, what is Job's view of God's justice?
options: God is just but beyond human understanding
questions.explanation: Job expresses that God's ways are beyond human comprehension, stating that God is 'wise in heart and mighty in strength' but His decisions are difficult for humans to understand (Job 9:4-10).

questions.text: How does Job describe God's power over the natural world in Job 9?
options: He commands the sun and moon
He alone spreads out the heavens and tramples the sea
questions.explanation: Job states that God stretches out the heavens, treads on the waves of the sea, and makes the constellations (Job 9:7-8), illustrating His supreme power over creation.

questions.text: What does Job say about God's justice in Job 9?
options: He is partial to the powerful
questions.explanation: Job acknowledges that God 'searches out the mind' and examines humans inwardly (Job 9:16-20), indicating God's just and thorough judgment.

questions.text: In Job 9, Job wishes to argue his case before God. What does he recognize about God's ability to be challenged?
options: He can be challenged and defeated
He is too powerful to challenge
questions.explanation: Job recognizes that no one can challenge God and succeed, emphasizing God's unmatched power (Job 9:4-10).

questions.text: What is Job's reaction to God's sovereignty as described in Job 9?
questions.explanation: Job humbly acknowledges God's sovereignty and His unrivaled power, recognizing that he cannot challenge or confront God (Job 9:4-10).

questions.text: Which natural elements does Job mention as evidence of God's power in Job 9?
questions.explanation: Job refers to God stretching out the heavens and trampling on the sea, highlighting His dominion over both sky and sea (Job 9:7-8).

questions.text: What does Job imply about human beings' ability to question God's decisions in Job 9?
questions.explanation: Job implies that no human can successfully question or challenge God's judgment due to His supreme power and wisdom (Job 9:4-10).

questions.text: Who is the prophet that received the message in Joel 1?
questions.explanation: The book begins with the words 'The word of the Lord that came to Joel,' identifying Joel as the prophet.

questions.text: What is described as being greatly feared in Joel 1:2-3?
questions.explanation: Joel emphasizes the importance of passing the message about the locust invasion from generation to generation (Joel 1:2-3).

questions.text: What is the main pest described as devastating the land in Joel 1?
questions.explanation: Joel describes a swarm of locusts that has consumed the fields, vineyards, and trees, symbolizing destruction (Joel 1:4).

questions.text: What should the priests do in response to the devastation, according to Joel 1:13?
options: Fasten belts and call for fasting
questions.explanation: The priestly response is to wear sackcloth and mourn, as a sign of grief and repentance (Joel 1:13).

questions.text: What does Joel call the people to do in Joel 1:14?
questions.explanation: Joel urges the people to consecrate a fast, call a sacred assembly, and pray to the Lord (Joel 1:14).

questions.text: What is one of the consequences of the locust invasion mentioned in Joel 1?
options: Wine and oil are dried up
questions.explanation: The invasion caused the wine and oil to wither, symbolizing economic and social distress (Joel 1:10).

questions.text: What does Joel compare the land's desolation to in Joel 1:10?
questions.explanation: Joel mentions the land is devastated 'because of the grain offering and drink offering are withheld,' implying drought and desolation (Joel 1:10).

questions.text: Which emotional response does Joel emphasize throughout Joel 1?
questions.explanation: Joel emphasizes lamentation and mourning in response to the devastation caused by the locusts and drought (Joel 1:8-12).

questions.text: What does Joel command the alarm to sound like in Joel 2:1?
questions.explanation: In Joel 2:1, the prophet instructs to sound the alarm like a trumpet to warn the people of approaching judgment.

questions.text: According to Joel 2:2, how is the day of the Lord described?
questions.explanation: Joel describes the day of the Lord as a day of darkness and gloom, emphasizing its severity and seriousness (Joel 2:2).

questions.text: What imagery does Joel use to describe the invading army in Joel 2:4-5?
questions.explanation: Joel describes the army as 'chariots like the fire' and their noise as a drone of a whirlwind, illustrating their power and speed (Joel 2:4-5).

questions.text: What will happen to the land as a result of the Lord’s judgment, according to Joel 2:10?
questions.explanation: Joel 2:10 states that the land will shake and tremble at the Lord’s coming, highlighting the earth-shaking nature of His judgment.

questions.text: What does Joel call for Israel to do in Joel 2:12-13?
options: Seek the Lord with all their heart
questions.explanation: Joel urges the people to return to the Lord with fasting, weeping, and mourning, emphasizing sincere repentance (Joel 2:12-13).

questions.text: What promise does God make to those who repent in Joel 2:28-29?
options: The Spirit will be poured out on all flesh
They will have peace on earth
questions.explanation: Joel 2:28-29 proclaims that God will pour out His Spirit on all people, empowering and calling them to serve Him, a central theme of revival and renewal.

questions.text: What is the main reason for God's warning and coming judgment in Joel 2?
options: For the sins of the nations
To bring justice and restore blessing
questions.explanation: While sin is involved, Joel emphasizes God's purpose of justice and restoring blessing for His people through His coming judgment (Joel 2:11).

questions.text: How does Joel describe the Lord in Joel 2:11?
questions.explanation: Joel describes God as 'a mighty warrior' who is executing His judgment and leading His army, emphasizing His power and authority (Joel 2:11).

questions.text: What does God promise to restore to Judah and Jerusalem in Joel 3?
questions.explanation: Joel 3:1-2 speaks about God restoring the inheritances of Judah and Jerusalem, emphasizing a future blessing of land and possessions.

questions.text: According to Joel 3, what will happen to the nations that oppress God’s people?
options: They will be judged and punished
They will convert to God's faith
questions.explanation: Joel 3:12-14 describes how God will judge the nations for oppressing His people, calling them to the Valley of Judgment.

questions.text: What imagery is used in Joel 3 to describe God's judgment during the Valley of Jehoshaphat?
questions.explanation: Joel 3:15-16 speaks of the Lord roaring from Zion and coming with fire and storm, symbolizing intense judgment and purification.

questions.text: What is the purpose of God gathering the nations in Joel 3?
questions.explanation: Joel 3:1-2 indicates God gathers the nations for judgment, specifically because they have harmed His people.

questions.text: According to Joel 3, what will happen to the people of Jerusalem in the day of the Lord’s coming?
options: They will be blessed and restored
questions.explanation: Joel 3:17 states that Jerusalem will be holy and no more will outsiders enter it, implying restoration and blessing for God's people.

questions.text: What does Joel say about the valley called 'Valley of Jehoshaphat'?
questions.explanation: Joel 3:12-14 describes the Valley of Jehoshaphat as the site where nations are gathered for judgment by God.

questions.text: What is one of the promises made about Jerusalem in Joel 3?
options: It will be holy and dwellings will be secure
It will be inhabited only by foreigners
questions.explanation: Joel 3:17 states that Jerusalem will be holy, and its dwelling will be secure, indicating peace and divine presence.

questions.text: Which theme is most prominent in Joel 3?
questions.explanation: Joel 3 centers on divine judgment of the nations and future restoration of Judah and Jerusalem, emphasizing God's sovereignty and mercy.

questions.text: What is described as being in the beginning according to John 1?
questions.explanation: John 1:1 states that 'In the beginning was the Word,' indicating the Word's eternal existence before creation.

questions.text: Who does John identify as the true light coming into the world?
questions.explanation: John 1:9 refers to Jesus as the true light that gives light to everyone, emphasizing His role as the spiritual illumination for the world.

questions.text: According to John 1, what was the Word’s relationship to God?
options: The Word is a messenger from God
The Word was with God and is God
The Word was created by God
The Word is simply a teaching
questions.explanation: John 1:1 states that 'The Word was with God, and the Word was God,' affirming the divine nature of the Word.

questions.text: How did the world respond to the Word according to John 1:10?
questions.explanation: John 1:10 explains that the world did not recognize or receive the Word when He came into the world.

questions.text: What did John the Baptist declare about Jesus in John 1?
options: He must increase, I must decrease
He is the Son of Man
questions.explanation: John 1:29 records John the Baptist calling Jesus the 'Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world,' recognizing His messianic role.

questions.text: What is the significance of Jesus being called 'the Word' in John 1?
options: He reveals God’s nature and will
questions.explanation: Referring to Jesus as 'the Word' signifies that He reveals God's very nature and communicates God's will to the world, as mentioned throughout John 1.

questions.text: According to John 1, what do those who received Jesus become?
questions.explanation: John 1:12 states that those who received Jesus have the right to become children of God, highlighting the spiritual rebirth and new identity available through faith.

questions.text: What is the main theme introduced at the beginning of John 1?
options: The divine nature of Jesus as the Word
The mission of John the Baptist
questions.explanation: The opening verses emphasize that Jesus, as the Word, is divine and existed from the beginning, establishing the core theme of His divine nature.

questions.text: What metaphor does Jesus use to describe Himself in John 10?
questions.explanation: In John 10, Jesus describes Himself as the 'Good Shepherd' who cares for His sheep (verse 11).

questions.text: According to John 10, what does the shepherd do for the sheep?
questions.explanation: The shepherd leads and cares for the sheep, guiding them and protecting them, as described in verses 3-4.

questions.text: In John 10, what significance is given to the sheep recognizing the shepherd's voice?
options: They obey him because of destination
They follow him because they know his voice
They stay close due to fear
They are summoned by sounding a bell
questions.explanation: The sheep recognize the shepherd’s voice and follow him, symbolizing believers' relationship with Christ (verse 4).

questions.text: What does Jesus say about His followers in John 10:27?
options: They hear His voice and follow Him
questions.explanation: Jesus states that His sheep hear His voice and follow Him, emphasizing a personal relationship (verse 27).

questions.text: According to John 10, what does Jesus say about His life and safety?
options: No one takes it from Him; He lays it down willingly
He will run away when threatened
He relies on others to protect Him
questions.explanation: Jesus affirms that He lays down His life voluntarily and that no one takes it from Him (verse 18).

questions.text: In John 10, what is the outcome for those who do not follow the Good Shepherd?
questions.explanation: Jesus mentions that apart from the shepherd, the sheep are scattered and vulnerable (verse 12).

questions.text: What does John 10 reveal about Jesus' authority over His own life?
options: He has authority to lay it down and take it up again
He depends on others for protection
He will be defeated by enemies
questions.explanation: Jesus states that He has authority to lay down His life and to take it up again, indicating divine authority (verse 18).

questions.text: Who was ill, prompting Jesus to travel to Bethany?
questions.explanation: Lazarus, the brother of Martha and Mary, was ill, leading them to send for Jesus (John 11:1-3).

questions.text: What did Jesus do when he heard about Lazarus' illness?
questions.explanation: Jesus intentionally delayed going to Bethany, stating that the illness would not end in death (John 11:6-7, 11).

questions.text: How did Martha respond when Jesus arrived in Bethany?
questions.explanation: Martha expressed faith in Jesus' power, saying she believed even now God would give whatever Jesus asked (John 11:21-22).

questions.text: What miracle did Jesus perform in John 11?
options: He raised Lazarus from the dead
questions.explanation: Jesus raised Lazarus from the dead, demonstrating his power over death (John 11:43-44).

questions.text: What reason did some give for believing Jesus could not raise Lazarus?
options: He was dead for four days
He was in a different town
questions.explanation: Some doubted because Lazarus had been in the tomb four days, suggesting decomposition (John 11:17, 39).

questions.text: What was the reaction of the crowd when Lazarus was raised?
questions.explanation: Many believed in Jesus, but others, especially the Pharisees, sought to kill him because of the miracle (John 11:45-53).

questions.text: What did Jesus say concerning Lazarus’ death and his purpose?
questions.explanation: Jesus called Lazarus' death 'sleep' to emphasize that he intended to bring him back to life, showing his authority over death (John 11:11-14).

questions.text: What was Jesus’ emotional response upon seeing Lazarus’ death?
questions.explanation: Jesus was deeply moved and wept, showing his compassion and genuine sorrow (John 11:35).

questions.text: Who anointed Jesus at Bethany in John 12?
questions.explanation: Mary of Bethany anointed Jesus' feet with perfume, as detailed in John 12:3.

questions.text: What did the disciples initially object to in John 12?
questions.explanation: Judas objected to Mary’s expensive perfume, worrying about the cost and distribution (John 12:4-6).

questions.text: What did Jesus say about the woman’s action in John 12?
options: She has anointed the Lord’s body
questions.explanation: Jesus states she has anointed His body for burial, indicating a prophetic act (John 12:7).

questions.text: What was the crowd's response to Jesus entering Jerusalem?
questions.explanation: The crowd greeted Jesus with palm branches and shouts of 'Hosanna,' celebrating His arrival (John 12:13).

questions.text: Why did many people believe in Jesus during this time?
options: Because they saw His signs and heard His words
questions.explanation: Many believed in Jesus after witnessing His signs and hearing His teachings, as noted in John 12:17-18.

questions.text: What did Jesus say about His death in John 12?
questions.explanation: Jesus spoke of His death as a form of glorification, indicating that His death would bring glory to the Son of Man (John 12:23-24).

questions.text: What does Jesus mean when He says, 'Unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies,'?
options: It will grow into a large plant
It must die to produce much fruit
questions.explanation: Jesus explains that His death is necessary for fruitful life, symbolizing His death and the growth of new life through resurrection (John 12:24).

questions.text: What does Jesus say about those who serve Him?
options: They will be where He is
questions.explanation: Jesus promises that those who serve Him will be with Him where He is and will be honored by the Father (John 12:26).

questions.text: What act does Jesus perform during the meal in John 13?
questions.explanation: In John 13, Jesus washes the disciples' feet to demonstrate humility and serve others (verse 5).

questions.text: Why does Jesus wash His disciples' feet?
questions.explanation: Jesus washes the disciples' feet to exemplify humility and servant leadership, urging His followers to do the same (verse 14-15).

questions.text: Who protests when Jesus begins to wash feet?
questions.explanation: Peter initially protests because he feels unworthy, but Jesus explains the importance of humility (verse 8).

questions.text: What new commandment does Jesus give in John 13?
options: Love one another as I have loved you
Believe in the Father and the Son
questions.explanation: Jesus commands His disciples to love one another just as He loved them, highlighting love as His new commandment (verse 34).

questions.text: Which disciple's loyalty is questioned during this chapter?
questions.explanation: Judas Iscariot's betrayal is foreshadowed, and Jesus knowing this reveals personal knowledge of Judas (verse 21-27).

questions.text: What does Jesus predict about Peter’s future during this chapter?
options: He will deny Him three times
questions.explanation: Jesus foretells that Peter will deny Him three times before the rooster crows, as recorded in verse 38.

questions.text: How does Jesus conclude His message in John 13?
options: By describing His death in detail
questions.explanation: Jesus concludes with a call to love one another and serve, setting the tone for His farewell teachings (verse 34).

questions.text: What does Jesus do after washing the disciples' feet?
options: He tells them to stay awake
questions.explanation: After washing their feet, Jesus dries them and takes His place again at the table, emphasizing service and humility (verse 12-17).

questions.text: What does Jesus tell his followers not to let their hearts be troubled about?
questions.explanation: Jesus assures His disciples not to let their hearts be troubled because He is going to prepare a place for them (John 14:1-3).

questions.text: According to John 14, what is the Father’s relationship to Jesus?
options: The Father and Jesus are the same person
The Father is in Jesus, and Jesus is in the Father
questions.explanation: Jesus states that the Father is in Him, and He is in the Father, emphasizing their unity (John 14:10-11).

questions.text: What promise does Jesus make regarding the Holy Spirit in John 14?
options: He will send the Holy Spirit as a Helper
The Holy Spirit will reveal all mysteries
The Holy Spirit will lead them into political leadership
They will understand all Scriptures immediately
questions.explanation: Jesus promises to send the Holy Spirit, referred to as the Helper, who will dwell with them and be in them (John 14:16-17).

questions.text: What does Jesus say about the way to the Father?
options: No one can come to the Father except through Jesus
questions.explanation: Jesus states that no one comes to the Father except through Him (John 14:6).

questions.text: How does Jesus describe the relationship between belief and His works?
options: His works are independent of belief
Believing in Him will also do the works He does and greater
Only the apostles can do His works
Works are not important in faith
questions.explanation: Jesus tells His disciples that they will do the works He has been doing and even greater works, through faith (John 14:12).

questions.text: What should believers ask for in Jesus' name, according to John 14?
questions.explanation: Jesus encourages them to ask for anything in His name so that the Father may be glorified through the Son (John 14:13).

questions.text: What assurance does Jesus give about His relationship with the Father when they ask in His name?
options: He will grant their requests to meet their needs
The Father will do whatever they ask in Jesus’ name
They will be blessed with material possessions
questions.explanation: Jesus states that the Father will do whatever is asked in His name, to glorify the Son (John 14:13-14).

questions.text: What does Jesus say about the peace He gives compared to the world’s peace?
options: His peace is temporary like the world’s
His peace is unlike the peace the world gives; it remains
His peace is only for believers in heaven
questions.explanation: Jesus offers a peace that the world cannot give, which remains with believers, unlike worldly peace that is temporary (John 14:27).

questions.text: What metaphor does Jesus use to describe himself in John 15:1?
questions.explanation: In John 15:1, Jesus describes himself as the 'true vine,' emphasizing the relationship between Him and His followers.

questions.text: According to John 15, what must a branch do to bear fruit?
questions.explanation: John 15:4 states that the branches must remain in Jesus, the vine, to bear fruit—highlighting dependence on Him.

questions.text: What is the consequence mentioned in John 15:6 for branches that do not remain in the vine?
options: They wither and are thrown away
questions.explanation: John 15:6 explains that branches not remaining in Jesus are cast away, wither, and are gathered for burning.

questions.text: What command does Jesus give about loving others in John 15?
options: Love one another as He loved us
questions.explanation: Jesus commands in John 15:12 that His followers should love one another as He has loved them.

questions.text: How does Jesus describe the relationship between the Father and the Son in John 15?
questions.explanation: In John 15:1, Jesus describes the Father as the 'vinedresser' or gardener, emphasizing their relationship, and He mentions the unity with the Father in verse 9, though the most direct relationship here is the vine and branches.

questions.text: What role do believers play in Jesus’ metaphor in John 15?
questions.explanation: Believers are the branches in the vine, as explained in John 15:5, emphasizing their dependence on Jesus for spiritual life and fruitfulness.

questions.text: What assurance does Jesus give about the world's treatment of His followers in John 15:18-19?
questions.explanation: John 15:18-19 explains that if the world hates Jesus, His followers should not be surprised, as they are not of the world, indicating persecution may come.

questions.text: What does Jesus say about the purpose of His commandments in John 15:10?
questions.explanation: In John 15:10, Jesus states that His commandments are given so that His followers may remain in His love, just as He remains in the Father’s love.

questions.text: What warning does Jesus give about the believers' future trials in John 16?
options: They will be persecuted and faced with trouble
They will always be accepted by the world
They will be exempt from suffering
questions.explanation: Jesus warns that believers will face persecution and tribulation, as stated in John 16:1-3. He prepares them for this reality to help them stand firm in their faith.

questions.text: According to John 16, what role will the Holy Spirit play when Jesus is gone?
options: He will convict of sin and guide into all truth
He will remain silent and inactive
He will replace Jesus as the Savior
questions.explanation: In John 16:8-13, Jesus explains that the Holy Spirit will convict the world of sin and guide believers into all truth, revealing what is to come.

questions.text: What does Jesus say about the grief of his followers when he departs?
options: It will turn into joy when they see Him again
It will be permanent and overwhelming
They will never see Him again
It will be as if they have lost everything
questions.explanation: Jesus acknowledges that believers will mourn his departure, but He also promises that their grief will turn into joy when they see Him again, as described in John 16:20-22.

questions.text: What is the significance of Jesus’ statement about asking in His name?
options: Believers will receive whatever they ask for in His name
It is a form of vain repetition
It applies only to the apostles
It guarantees all requests will be granted
questions.explanation: In John 16:23-24, Jesus teaches that believers can ask the Father directly in His name, and they will receive, highlighting the importance of prayer aligned with His authority.

questions.text: How does Jesus describe the world's reaction to His followers in John 16?
options: They will hate and persecute them
They will welcome and embrace them
They will misunderstand them but tolerate them
questions.explanation: Jesus states in John 16:2 that the world will hate believers because they do not belong to the world, and persecutions will come as a result.

questions.text: What comfort does Jesus give regarding his departure and the work of the Holy Spirit?
options: The Spirit will bring peace and understanding
They will forget Jesus after He leaves
The Holy Spirit will replace Jesus physically
Their work will cease after Jesus departs
questions.explanation: Jesus assures that the Holy Spirit will help, teach, and remind the disciples of His words, bringing peace and understanding as He departs, as seen in John 16:13 and 16:33.

questions.text: In John 16, what does Jesus promise about the joy of his followers?
options: Their sorrow will be turned into joy
They will only have temporary happiness
Joy is only for those who follow perfectly
Joy will come after trials fade away
questions.explanation: Jesus tells his disciples that their sorrow during His absence will turn into joy when they see Him again, emphasizing the future hope of resurrection and reunion (John 16:20-22).

questions.text: How should believers respond to the challenges Jesus describes in John 16?
options: Trust in the Holy Spirit and remain steadfast
questions.explanation: Jesus encourages believers to trust in the Holy Spirit's guidance and remain faithful amid challenges, knowing that their sorrow will eventually turn into joy (John 16:33).

questions.text: Who does Jesus say gives Him authority to finish His work in John 17?
questions.explanation: In John 17:2, Jesus mentions that the Father has granted Him authority over all people to give eternal life. This highlights the divine authority granted by the Father to the Son.

questions.text: What does Jesus pray for His disciples regarding their unity?
questions.explanation: In John 17:21, Jesus prays that His disciples may be one, just as He and the Father are one, emphasizing spiritual unity among believers.

questions.text: According to Jesus' prayer, who is 'glorified' in Himself?
questions.explanation: In John 17:1-2, Jesus speaks of praying to be glorified so He can glorify the Father, indicating that the Son is to be glorified in Himself as part of His divine mission.

questions.text: What does Jesus express about the eternal life He gives?
questions.explanation: In John 17:3, Jesus defines eternal life as knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ, highlighting relational knowledge over mere existence.

questions.text: In His prayer, Jesus requests protection for whom?
questions.explanation: John 17:11, Jesus prays specifically for His disciples to be kept safe, indicating His concern for their spiritual protection.

questions.text: How does Jesus describe those who are not of the world in His prayer?
questions.explanation: In John 17:9, Jesus states that He is not praying for the world but for those whom the Father has given Him, implying they are chosen by God.

questions.text: What is Jesus' ultimate purpose in praying for His followers?
options: That they may have His joy fulfilled in themselves
questions.explanation: In John 17:13, Jesus prays that His followers may have His joy fulfilled in themselves, emphasizing spiritual joy as part of His purpose.

questions.text: What does Jesus say about the world in His prayer?
questions.explanation: In John 17:14, Jesus states that He has given His followers God's word and the world hates them because they are not of the world, highlighting opposition from the world.

questions.text: Where does Jesus go after praying in the garden according to John 18?
questions.explanation: Jesus is led to the Jewish leaders after his arrest in the garden (John 18:12-13).

questions.text: Whom does Peter incorrectly identify as the servant of the high priest in John 18?
questions.explanation: Peter cuts off Malchus's ear, identifying him as the servant of the high priest (John 18:10-11).

questions.text: Who betrayed Jesus according to John 18?
questions.explanation: Judas Iscariot betrayed Jesus, leading to his arrest in the garden (John 18:2-5).

questions.text: What does Jesus say when asked if he is the King in John 18?
options: My kingdom is not of this world
questions.explanation: Jesus affirms, 'You say that I am' when questioned about being the King (John 18:37).

questions.text: Which Roman official questions Jesus during his trial in John 18?
questions.explanation: Pontius Pilate questions Jesus about his kingship and truth (John 18:28-38).

questions.text: What does Jesus say about his kingdom during his trial in John 18?
options: My kingdom is of this world
My kingdom is from another place
questions.explanation: Jesus states that his kingdom is not of this world, emphasizing a spiritual realm (John 18:36).

questions.text: How does Peter react when he is recognized as a follower of Jesus in John 18?
options: He denies knowing Jesus three times
questions.explanation: Peter denies knowing Jesus three times before the rooster crows (John 18:17-27).

questions.text: What does Jesus say about his followers during his arrest in John 18?
options: My followers are not of this world
questions.explanation: Jesus indicates that his followers belong to a spiritual realm different from worldly powers (John 18:36).

questions.text: Who was responsible for sentencing Jesus to be crucified?
questions.explanation: Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor, authorized Jesus' crucifixion as recorded in John 19:1-16. Despite finding no guilt in Jesus, he ultimately handed Him over for execution to satisfy the crowd.

questions.text: What specific physical action did Pilate take to symbolize his decision?
options: He placed a crown on Jesus
questions.explanation: Pilate washed his hands in front of the crowd, symbolizing that he was innocent of Jesus' blood (John 19:24). This act was a traditional way to show that he did not want responsibility for Jesus’ death.

questions.text: What was written on the sign placed above Jesus on the cross?
questions.explanation: The sign read 'Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews,' which was intended as an inscription by Pilate, as recorded in John 19:19-22.

questions.text: Who was present at Jesus' crucifixion according to this chapter?
options: His mother and the beloved disciple
questions.explanation: John 19:25-27 describes Jesus' mother, Mary, and the disciple Jesus loved (traditionally understood as John) present at the cross, caring for each other.

questions.text: What did Jesus say before He died?
questions.explanation: Jesus declared 'It is finished' (John 19:30), signifying the completion of His mission and the fulfillment of Scripture.

questions.text: What did the soldiers do after Jesus’ death?
questions.explanation: The soldiers pierced Jesus' side with a spear to confirm His death, as described in John 19:34.

questions.text: Who asked Pilate for Jesus’ body and prepared it for burial?
questions.explanation: Joseph of Arimathea requested Jesus’ body and, along with Nicodemus, prepared it according to Jewish burial customs (John 19:38).

questions.text: What was placed in Jesus’ tomb after His death?
questions.explanation: Jesus' body was wrapped in linen cloth and laid in a new tomb, which was then sealed with a large stone (John 19:41-42).

questions.text: Where does the wedding happen in John 2?
questions.explanation: The miracle occurs at a wedding in Cana of Galilee, as mentioned in verse 1.

questions.text: What problem arises at the wedding in Cana?
questions.explanation: Verse 3 states they ran out of wine, prompting Jesus’s first miracle.

questions.text: What did Jesus instruct the servants to do with the jars of water?
options: Take to the master of the feast
questions.explanation: Jesus told them to take the water to the master of the feast, which then turned into wine (verse 8).

questions.text: What was the significance of Jesus' miracle at the wedding?
questions.explanation: This miracle reveals Jesus' divine authority and is considered his first sign, pointing to his identity (verse 11).

questions.text: How did Jesus respond to his mother’s request regarding the wine?
options: He said, ‘My time has not yet come’
questions.explanation: Jesus replied that his time had not yet come, but still performed the miracle (verse 4).

questions.text: What does the miracle at Cana teach about Jesus’ ministry?
options: He reveals his divine power gradually
questions.explanation: This event illustrates that Jesus' divine power is revealed at specific times to fulfill God's purpose, not immediately for all to see (verse 11).

questions.text: What is the symbolic significance of the water turning into wine?
options: The transformation of old to new
questions.explanation: The miracle signifies the transition from the old covenant to the new covenant through Jesus, symbolizing spiritual transformation (verse 11).

questions.text: Why is Jesus' first miracle considered a 'sign' in the Gospel of John?
questions.explanation: This miracle serves as a sign pointing to Jesus’ divine identity and mission, which is emphasized throughout the Gospel of John (verse 11).

questions.text: Who discovered Jesus' empty tomb first in John 20?
questions.explanation: Mary Magdalene was the first to find the tomb empty, as noted in John 20:1-2.

questions.text: What did Mary Magdalene see when she looked into the tomb?
questions.explanation: Mary Magdalene saw two angels sitting where Jesus' body had been, as described in John 20:11-12.

questions.text: How did Peter and the other disciple respond after hearing about the empty tomb?
questions.explanation: Peter and the other disciple ran to the tomb to see for themselves, as detailed in John 20:3-5.

questions.text: What did the other disciple see but not enter into the tomb?
questions.explanation: The other disciple saw the linen wrappings lying there, but did not go inside, as noted in John 20:6-7.

questions.text: Who believed after seeing the empty tomb but before seeing Jesus?
questions.explanation: The other disciple believed after observing the empty tomb, as stated in John 20:8.

questions.text: Where did Jesus appear to the disciples for the first time?
questions.explanation: Jesus appeared in the upper room where the disciples were gathered, as described in John 20:19.

questions.text: Where were some of the disciples fishing when Jesus appeared to them after His resurrection?
questions.explanation: The disciples were fishing on the Sea of Galilee, as mentioned in John 21:1.

questions.text: What was Jesus doing when the disciples recognized Him on the shore?
questions.explanation: Jesus was preparing breakfast and cooking fish when the disciples saw Him on the shore (John 21:9).

questions.text: What command did Jesus give to Peter after the miraculous catch of fish?
questions.explanation: Jesus told Peter to 'Feed my sheep,' emphasizing the care and leadership Peter would have (John 21:17).

questions.text: What did Jesus do that demonstrated His care for His disciples during the breakfast on the shore?
questions.explanation: Jesus prepared and provided breakfast for the disciples, showing His care and provision (John 21:9).

questions.text: How did Peter respond when he recognized Jesus while fishing?
questions.explanation: Peter recognized Jesus and then hastily responded by swimming to the shore (John 21:7).

questions.text: What was Jesus' instruction to the disciples regarding their fishing efforts?
options: Cast the net on the left side
Cast the net on the right side
Put down your nets and follow me
questions.explanation: Jesus instructed them to cast their net on the right side of the boat, which led to the miraculous catch (John 21:6).

questions.text: What does the seven disciples' presence during breakfast signify in the context of this passage?
questions.explanation: Their gathering around Jesus for breakfast signifies fellowship and the restored relationship after His resurrection (John 21:12-13).

questions.text: Who is involved in the conversation with Jesus in John 3?
questions.explanation: Nicodemus, a Pharisee, comes to Jesus at night to ask about spiritual matters (John 3:1-2).

questions.text: What must one do to see the kingdom of God, according to Jesus in John 3?
questions.explanation: Jesus states that one must be born again to see the kingdom of God (John 3:3).

questions.text: What does Jesus compare being born again to in John 3?
options: A new birth from water and Spirit
questions.explanation: Jesus explains that one must be born of water and Spirit to enter God's kingdom (John 3:5).

questions.text: What analogy does Jesus use to explain faith in the Son of Man in John 3?
options: Lifting up the serpent in the wilderness
questions.explanation: Jesus references Moses lifting up the serpent so that everyone who looks upon it is healed, as an analogy for the Son of Man being lifted up (John 3:14-15).

questions.text: What is the result for those who believe in Jesus, according to John 3?
