questions.explanation: John 3:16 states that belief in Jesus grants eternal life to believers.

questions.text: What does Jesus say about the world in John 3 when it comes to condemning it?
options: The world is waiting for salvation
The world is judged after death
questions.explanation: Jesus indicates that the world is already under condemnation because of its unbelief (John 3:18).

questions.text: According to John 3, why did God send His Son into the world?
options: To save the world through Him
questions.explanation: John 3:17 states that God sent His Son not to condemn but to save the world through Him.

questions.text: What must one do to avoid perishing but have everlasting life, as described in John 3?
questions.explanation: The key message of John 3:16-18 is that belief in Jesus grants eternal life and avoids perishing.

questions.text: Where does Jesus meet the Samaritan woman?
questions.explanation: Jesus meets the woman at Jacob's well, as described in John 4:6.

questions.text: What does Jesus request from the Samaritan woman?
questions.explanation: Jesus asks for a drink of water from the woman at the well (John 4:7).

questions.text: Why is it surprising that Jesus talks to the woman?
questions.explanation: Jewish men typically did not converse publicly with Samaritan women, making Jesus' dialogue noteworthy (John 4:9).

questions.text: What does Jesus reveal about his mission to the woman?
options: He came to offer living water
He came to overthrow Roman rule
He was the son of man
questions.explanation: Jesus speaks of offering 'living water,' symbolizing eternal life (John 4:10).

questions.text: How does the woman initially respond to Jesus' offer of living water?
options: She shows interest and asks for it
She questions the need for a drink
She ignores him and walks away
questions.explanation: The woman questions, 'How can you give me water?' showing curiosity but also confusion (John 4:11-12).

questions.text: What does Jesus reveal about her personal life?
questions.explanation: Jesus mentions her history of five husbands and current situation, revealing his knowledge of her personal life (John 4:16-18).

questions.text: What does the woman do after her encounter with Jesus?
options: She goes into her town to tell others
She takes water to her home
questions.explanation: The woman goes back to her town to share her experience and testify about Jesus (John 4:28-29).

questions.text: What is the key theme of John 4?
options: Jesus offering living water and salvation
questions.explanation: The chapter emphasizes Jesus offering 'living water,' symbolizing eternal life and salvation for all people, including Samaritans (John 4:10-14).

questions.text: What event is described as happening at the pool of Bethesda in John 5?
questions.explanation: Jesus heals a man who had been an invalid for 38 years at the pool of Bethesda, as described in John 5:1-9.

questions.text: Why was the man at the pool unable to get into the water?
questions.explanation: The man was paralyzed and unable to move into the pool himself, as stated in John 5:3-5.

questions.text: What did Jesus instruct the man to do after healing him?
options: Pick up his bed and walk
questions.explanation: Jesus told the man to pick up his bed and walk, which he did immediately (John 5:8-9).

questions.text: What was the controversy the Jews had regarding Jesus' healing on the Sabbath?
questions.explanation: The Jews accused Jesus of breaking the Sabbath law because he healed on that day (John 5:10-16).

questions.text: How does Jesus justify his healing in John 5:19-20?
options: He claims he has special powers
He says the Father is working
questions.explanation: Jesus states that the Father is always working and that he, too, is doing his Father’s work (John 5:17-19).

questions.text: What does Jesus say about his authority in John 5:26?
options: He has received it from the Spirit
He has authority from the crowd
questions.explanation: Jesus states that he has life in himself, indicating his divine authority (John 5:26).

questions.text: What warning does Jesus give about those who hear his word and believe?
questions.explanation: Jesus promises that those who believe in him will have eternal life and will not come into judgment (John 5:24).

questions.text: What event is described at the beginning of John 6 that attracted a large crowd?
questions.explanation: John 6 opens with Jesus feeding the five thousand, which is a significant miracle recorded in verses 1-14.

questions.text: How many loaves and fishes were used to feed the crowd according to John 6?
questions.explanation: Verses 9 states that there were five barley loaves and two fishes used to feed the crowd.

questions.text: What did Jesus do immediately after feeding the five thousand?
options: He crossed the Sea of Galilee
He went to the mountains alone
He taught about the kingdom of God
questions.explanation: After the miracle, Jesus instructed His disciples to cross the Sea of Galilee, as highlighted in verses 16-21.

questions.text: What did Jesus declare himself to be in John 6 that caused confusion among the crowd?
questions.explanation: In verses 35 and 48, Jesus states, 'I am the bread of life,' which was central to His teaching in this chapter.

questions.text: What did many of Jesus’ followers do after His teaching about eating His flesh and drinking His blood?
options: They left Him and stopped following
questions.explanation: Verses 66-67 mention that many disciples turned away and no longer followed Jesus after His difficult teachings.

questions.text: In John 6, what does Jesus say is the food that leads to eternal life?
options: Himself as the bread of life
questions.explanation: Jesus emphasizes that believing in Him as the bread of life is essential for eternal life, particularly in verses 35 and 54.

questions.text: What miracle does Jesus perform to demonstrate His power over nature in John 6?
questions.explanation: In verses 16-21, Jesus walks on the sea to His disciples, showing His authority over natural elements.

questions.text: What is the main theme of John 6?
options: The bread of life and eternal salvation
questions.explanation: John 6 focuses on Jesus identifying Himself as the bread of life and calls for belief in Him as the source of eternal life.

questions.text: Where was Jesus during John 7?
questions.explanation: Jesus traveled to Jerusalem for the Feast of Tabernacles, which is mentioned in John 7:10–14.

questions.text: Why did Jesus' brothers encourage Him to go to Judea?
questions.explanation: His brothers urged Jesus to go to Judea so His works could be seen publicly, as they said, 'Show yourself to the world' (John 7:4).

questions.text: Why did Jesus initially not go to Judea publicly?
options: His time had not yet come
questions.explanation: Jesus said His time had not yet come, so He did not go publicly at that moment (John 7:6–8).

questions.text: What was Jesus doing at the Feast of Tabernacles before going into the temple?
questions.explanation: Jesus was teaching in the temple, but the Jews were wondering if He was the Christ (John 7:14–15).

questions.text: How did the crowd react to Jesus’ teaching in the temple?
questions.explanation: The crowd was divided, with some questioning if He was the Christ and others skeptical, indicating differing opinions (John 7:12).

questions.text: What did Jesus say about His teaching in John 7?
questions.explanation: Jesus said His teaching was from Him, indicating divine authority, and not His own (John 7:16).

questions.text: How did Jesus compare His origin to that of His critics?
options: They know Him but reject Him
They do not know where He is from
questions.explanation: Jesus stated His origin was from the one who sent Him, implying divine authority, but His critics claimed they knew where He was from, showing their misunderstanding (John 7:28–29).

questions.text: What was the outcome of Jesus' teaching during the feast?
questions.explanation: The crowd was divided, and some sought to seize Him, indicating a mixed response to His teachings (John 7:32–44).

questions.text: What did Jesus say to the accusers after they presented the woman?
options: Let him who is without sin cast the first stone
questions.explanation: Jesus responded, 'Let him who is without sin cast the first stone,' challenging their judgment and highlighting God's mercy (John 8:7).

questions.text: What did Jesus say after the woman was spared from punishment?
questions.explanation: Jesus told the woman to go and sin no more, emphasizing repentance and a new beginning (John 8:11).

questions.text: What assertion does Jesus make about Himself in John 8:12?
options: I am the way, the truth, and the life
I am the bread of life
I am the light of the world
I am the resurrection and the life
questions.explanation: In John 8:12, Jesus declares, 'I am the light of the world,' asserting His divine role in providing spiritual illumination.

questions.text: How do the Pharisees respond to Jesus’ claim in John 8:13?
questions.explanation: The Pharisees challenge Jesus, questioning the legitimacy of His testimony, as seen in John 8:13.

questions.text: What does Jesus say about His testimony in John 8:14?
questions.explanation: Jesus explains that His testimony is valid because it is from the Father, emphasizing divine authority (John 8:14-16).

questions.text: What freedom does Jesus offer to those who follow Him in John 8:31-32?
questions.explanation: Jesus promises that those who abide in His word will know the truth and be truly free from sin (John 8:31-32).

questions.text: How do the people react to Jesus’ teaching about knowing the truth in John 8:59?
options: They pick up stones to kill Him
questions.explanation: The people attempt to kill Jesus by stoneing Him, because He claimed equality with God, escalating the conflict (John 8:59).

questions.text: What was the man's physical condition when he was born?
questions.explanation: According to John 9:1, the man was born blind, which prompted the disciples' question about sin and suffering.

questions.text: What did Jesus do to heal the man born blind?
questions.explanation: In John 9:6, Jesus spat on the ground, made mud with his saliva, and anointed the man's eyes, instructing him to wash in the Pool of Siloam.

questions.text: Where did the man go after Jesus instructed him to wash?
questions.explanation: Jesus told the man to go and wash in the Pool of Siloam, which he did, leading to his sight being restored (John 9:7).

questions.text: How did the neighbors react after the man was healed?
options: They told him to keep quiet
questions.explanation: In John 9:8-9, neighbors were surprised and questioned whether the man was the same person who was born blind, showing doubt and curiosity.

questions.text: How did the Pharisees respond to the man’s healing on the Sabbath?
questions.explanation: In John 9:13-16, the Pharisees examined the man and debated whether Jesus could be from God because he healed on the Sabbath, showing suspicion.

questions.text: What was the man’s testimony about how he received his sight?
questions.explanation: The man consistently testified that Jesus had healed him, telling the people and Pharisees that Jesus made mud and opened his eyes (John 9:11).

questions.text: What was the conclusion of the Pharisees about Jesus after questioning the healed man?
questions.explanation: The Pharisees claimed that Jesus could not be from God because he healed on the Sabbath, which they considered a violation of tradition (John 9:16).

questions.text: How did the healed man view Jesus at the end of the chapter?
questions.explanation: In John 9:17, the man calls Jesus a prophet, acknowledging his divine role in his healing after questioning him about Jesus’ identity.

questions.text: Who commissioned Jonah to go to Nineveh?
questions.explanation: God commanded Jonah to go to Nineveh, as stated in Jonah 1:1, 'The word of the Lord came to Jonah.'

questions.text: Where was Jonah when he received God's command?
questions.explanation: Jonah was on a ship heading to Tarshish, near Joppa, when he received God's command (Jonah 1:3).

questions.text: What did Jonah do in response to God's command?
options: He obeyed and went to Nineveh
questions.explanation: Jonah chose to flee from God's presence by sailing to Tarshish, as described in Jonah 1:3.

questions.text: What action did Jonah take to try to escape God's plan?
options: He paid a fare to sail to Tarshish
questions.explanation: Jonah paid a fare and boarded a ship heading to Tarshish to escape God's calling (Jonah 1:3).

questions.text: What was the destination Jonah initially tried to reach?
questions.explanation: Jonah set out for Tarshish, a distant place in the opposite direction of Nineveh, as per Jonah 1:3.

questions.text: What was the primary reason Jonah chose to run away?
options: He wanted to sail to Tarshish
questions.explanation: Jonah disobeyed God's specific command to go to Nineveh, choosing instead to flee to Tarshish (Jonah 1:3).

questions.text: What does Jonah's attempt to flee reveal about his initial attitude?
options: He was eager to obey God
He was reluctant to go to Nineveh
He was indifferent about God's command
He wanted to see the world
questions.explanation: Jonah’s attempt to flee indicates reluctance or hesitation to obey God's command to go to Nineveh (Jonah 1:3).

questions.text: Which sea or body of water is involved in Jonah’s story in this chapter?
questions.explanation: Jonah’s story involves the Mediterranean Sea, where the ship was sailing when he attempted to flee (Jonah 1:3).

questions.text: In Jonah 2, where does Jonah pray to God?
questions.explanation: Jonah prays to God from inside the fish's belly, as described in Jonah 2:1-2.

questions.text: What does Jonah recognize about God in his prayer?
options: He is the God of the mountains
He is the God of the sea
He is the Lord my God
He is the God of lightning
questions.explanation: Jonah acknowledges that 'You, Lord, my God,' are the true God, showing his recognition of God's sovereignty as seen in Jonah 2:7.

questions.text: What imagery does Jonah use to describe his situation?
options: He was in a lion's den
He was in the depths of the ocean
He was in a pit of destruction
questions.explanation: Jonah describes being 'deeper than the depths' and the seaweed wrapped around him, depicting his struggle in the sea, consistent with Jonah 2:5-6.

questions.text: What plea does Jonah make in his prayer?
questions.explanation: Jonah prays for salvation, acknowledging that salvation belongs to the Lord, as seen in Jonah 2:9.

questions.text: What does Jonah declare about God's response to his prayer?
options: God hears his voice from the deep
questions.explanation: Jonah declares that God heard his cry from the depths, indicating God's attentive response as in Jonah 2:2 and 2:7.

questions.text: What symbol of deliverance does Jonah mention at the end of his prayer?
questions.explanation: Jonah refers to being rescued from the fish, which symbolizes God's deliverance, especially in Jonah 2:10.

questions.text: How does Jonah describe his attitude before praying?
questions.explanation: Jonah describes himself as sinking into the depths and feeling overwhelmed, which prompted his prayer (Jonah 2:3-4).

questions.text: What eventual action does Jonah take after praying?
options: He is vomited onto dry land
He falls asleep in the fish
questions.explanation: God commands the fish to vomit Jonah onto dry land, allowing him to continue his mission, as described in Jonah 2:10.

questions.text: What did Jonah do after hearing God's command in Jonah 3?
options: Went to Nineveh to proclaim God's message
Built an altar to worship God
Prayed for forgiveness in the city
questions.explanation: In Jonah 3, Jonah obeys God's command and goes to Nineveh to deliver God's message (verse 3).

questions.text: How did the people of Nineveh respond to Jonah's message?
options: They demanded proof of God's power
questions.explanation: The people of Nineveh believed God, declared a fast, and repented, turning from their evil ways (verses 5-8).

questions.text: What specific action did the king of Nineveh take upon hearing Jonah's message?
options: He called for a fast and repentance
He offered sacrifices to pagan gods
questions.explanation: The king proclaimed a fast, called for everyone to turn from evil, and to seek mercy from God (verse 7-8).

questions.text: What did God do when He saw the people's response in Nineveh?
options: Withdrew His judgment and spared the city
Sent a second prophet to confirm his message
Plagued the city with a storm
questions.explanation: God saw their repentance and compassionately relented from bringing disaster, showing His mercy (verse 10).

questions.text: How is Nineveh described in Jonah 3?
questions.explanation: Nineveh is described as a great city to God, emphasizing its importance and the significance of God's mercy shown to it (verse 3).

questions.text: What does Jonah’s obedience to God's command in this chapter demonstrate about him?
options: His reluctance to follow God's will
His initial disobedience but eventual obedience
questions.explanation: Jonah’s going to Nineveh to deliver God's message shows his obedience, even though he initially hesitated, demonstrating a change in response (verses 1-4).

questions.text: What was Jonah’s original reaction to God's command to go to Nineveh?
questions.explanation: Initially, Jonah was reluctant and tried to flee from God's command, which is described in earlier chapters (not directly in Jonah 3, but implied by his previous actions).

questions.text: What is the main theme of Jonah 3?
options: The importance of obedience and repentance
questions.explanation: Jonah 3 highlights the importance of obedience to God and sincere repentance, as shown by the people of Nineveh turning from their evil ways and God’s mercy towards them.

questions.text: How did Jonah react to God's mercy toward Nineveh?
options: He was displeased and became angry
He stayed silent and did not react
questions.explanation: Jonah was displeased and became angry because he did not want God to show mercy to Nineveh (Jonah 4:1-2).

questions.text: What plant provided shade for Jonah in the story?
questions.explanation: God caused a plant, described as a vine, to grow overnight, providing shade for Jonah (Jonah 4:6).

questions.text: Why did Jonah become angry about the plant?
options: It withered quickly, leaving him exposed
He cared more about the plant than people
He was worried about its survival
questions.explanation: Jonah was angry because he cared about the plant's shade more than the salvation of Nineveh, revealing his selfishness (Jonah 4:8-9).

questions.text: What did God use to teach Jonah a lesson at the end of the chapter?
questions.explanation: God used the contrast between the plant's growth and withering, along with the worm, to teach Jonah about compassion and God's mercy (Jonah 4:6-11).

questions.text: What was Jonah’s complaint about God's actions?
options: He thought God was too severe
He was upset that God saved Nineveh
He was angry because the prophet was ignored
questions.explanation: Jonah was angry because he believed that God's mercy towards Nineveh was undeserved and unjust (Jonah 4:1-2).

questions.text: How did God demonstrate His compassion in Jonah 4?
options: By providing shade and then sparing Nineveh
By sending a prophet to warn Jonah
questions.explanation: God demonstrated His compassion by sparing Nineveh from destruction and showing mercy, which displeased Jonah (Jonah 4:10-11).

questions.text: What does Jonah’s reaction reveal about his character?
options: His selfishness and lack of compassion
questions.explanation: Jonah's anger and displeasure reveal his selfishness and lack of compassion towards Nineveh, contrasting with God's mercy (Jonah 4:1-4).

questions.text: What was Jonah’s main concern at the end of the chapter?
options: That he would lose his prophetic authority
That his own life was in danger
questions.explanation: Jonah was concerned that Nineveh's repentance would lead to God's mercy being extended to them, thus preventing their destruction (Jonah 4:1-3).

questions.text: Who died and was buried in Joshua 1:1?
questions.explanation: Moses died and was buried in the land of Moab, as stated at the beginning of Joshua 1, marking the transition of leadership to Joshua.

questions.text: What command does God give Joshua in Joshua 1:6?
questions.explanation: God commands Joshua to be strong and courageous multiple times in Joshua 1, emphasizing confidence in obeying His law (Joshua 1:6).

questions.text: According to Joshua 1:8, what should not depart from your mouth?
questions.explanation: Joshua is instructed to keep the Book of the Law always on his mouth, meditating on it day and night (Joshua 1:8), emphasizing the importance of scripture in daily life.

questions.text: What promise does God make to Joshua in Joshua 1:5?
options: No one will stand before you
questions.explanation: God assures Joshua that as He was with Moses, so He will be with Joshua, and no one will stand against him (Joshua 1:5).

questions.text: How does Joshua respond to God's command in Joshua 1:10?
questions.explanation: Joshua prepares the officers to go through the camp and command the people, indicating readiness and obedience (Joshua 1:10).

questions.text: What is the people’s response in Joshua 1:16-17?
questions.explanation: The Israelites agree to follow Joshua’s leadership, emphasizing their commitment and trust in him as their leader (Joshua 1:16-17).

questions.text: What is Joshua instructed to do in Joshua 1:7 regarding the law?
questions.explanation: Joshua is told to be strong and very courageous, carefully obeying all the law and not turning from it in any way (Joshua 1:7).

questions.text: Which geographical area is Joshua instructed to lead the Israelites into?
questions.explanation: Joshua is called to lead the Israelites into the Promised Land, which is Canaan (Joshua 1:2).

questions.text: Who was the king of Jerusalem that attacked Gibeon after hearing about Joshua's victory?
questions.explanation: The king of Jerusalem who attacked Gibeon was Adonizedek (Joshua 10:1).

questions.text: What was Joshua's prayer when the sun was about to set during battle?
questions.explanation: Joshua prayed for the sun to stand still so they could complete the victory (Joshua 10:12-13).

questions.text: How long did the sun remain in the sky during Joshua's prayer?
questions.explanation: The sun stood still until Joshua defeated the Amorite kings, lengthening the day (Joshua 10:13).

questions.text: What did Joshua do after defeating the kings?
questions.explanation: Joshua hanged the kings on trees until evening and then used large stones to bury them (Joshua 10:24-26).

questions.text: Which geographic area is primarily involved in Joshua 10?
questions.explanation: The events involving the kings and battles take place in southern Canaan, including Jerusalem and Gibeon areas (Joshua 10).

questions.text: What was the outcome of the battle for Gibeon?
questions.explanation: Gibeon successfully called for help, and Israel came to their aid, resulting in a victory (Joshua 10:6-8).

questions.text: What was Joshua's main focus during this chapter?
questions.explanation: Joshua led Israel in a series of military campaigns against the southern Canaanite kings (Joshua 10).

questions.text: Who was the king of Hazor that Joshua’s army defeated?
questions.explanation: Joshua 11:1 mentions Jabin, the king of Hazor, whom Joshua defeated in battle.

questions.text: What did the Israelites do after conquering the cities in Joshua 11?
questions.explanation: Joshua 11:11 states that they burned the cities, including Hazor, as part of the conquest.

questions.text: Which city did Joshua lay siege to and conquer, according to Joshua 11?
questions.explanation: Hazor was the major city captured by Joshua in Joshua 11, as described throughout the chapter.

questions.text: How did Joshua deal with the remaining kings and cities after the main battles?
questions.explanation: Joshua 11 details that Joshua destroyed the kings and their cities after defeating them in battle.

questions.text: What strategic military role did the kings of the Hittites play, as seen in Joshua 11?
questions.explanation: Joshua 11:1-5 describes how various kings, including those of the Hittites, fought against Israel, but were defeated.

questions.text: Where did the Israelites capture the cities as part of their campaign in Joshua 11?
options: Among the cities of the north
questions.explanation: Joshua 11 describes northern cities, including Hazor, being captured during the campaign.

questions.text: What was Joshua’s overall military strategy in Joshua 11?
questions.explanation: Joshua's strategy involved quick and decisive attacks on the armies of the kings, leading to the conquest of their cities, as seen in Joshua 11.

questions.text: What does Joshua 11 teach about God's role in military victories?
options: God's guidance and power enabled victory
Victory depended solely on Israel’s numbers
God told them to avoid fighting
questions.explanation: Throughout Joshua 11, God's intervention and assurance are implied as key factors in Israel’s victorious campaigns.

questions.text: What does Joshua 12 primarily list?
options: The tribes of Israel in their land
questions.explanation: Joshua 12 details the kings defeated by Israel and their lands, summarizing Israel's victories. It lists the kings and territories conquered under Moses and Joshua (verses 1-7).

questions.text: Which king was listed as conquered by Joshua?
questions.explanation: Joshua defeated the king of Hazor, as listed among the kings conquered under his leadership (verse 7).

questions.text: Which territory did the king of Jericho rule over?
questions.explanation: The king of Jericho ruled over the city of Jericho, which was among the first Jericho conquered by Israel (verse 21).

questions.text: Which king was defeated in the region of the Jordan and the south?
questions.explanation: The king of Hormah is listed among the defeated kings in the southern regions (verse 14).

questions.text: What was the purpose of Joshua 12 as a chapter?
options: To describe the laws given to Israel
To list the conquests of Israel
To recount the leadership of Joshua
To describe the divisions of the land
questions.explanation: Joshua 12 serves as a summary listing the kings defeated by Israel and their territories, highlighting Israel’s victories (verses 1-24).

questions.text: How does Joshua 12 conclude?
options: It summarizes the conquest of all lands
It lists the remaining territory to be conquered
It provides detailed laws for each tribe
questions.explanation: The chapter concludes with a summary of Israel's victorious conquests, essentially summarizing all the kings and lands subdued (verse 24).

questions.text: Which statement best describes Joshua 12?
options: A record of laws given to Israel
A compilation of Israel's victories over kings
A narrative of Joshua’s personal journey
questions.explanation: Joshua 12 is a summary listing the kings defeated by Israel, emphasizing their military victories and territorial conquests.

questions.text: Who is identified as the existing leader of Israel at the beginning of Joshua 13?
questions.explanation: Joshua is recognized as the leader of Israel as he prepares to take possession of the remaining land (verse 1).

questions.text: What task is Joshua commanded to do regarding the land still unconquered?
options: Divide and allocate the rest of the land
questions.explanation: Joshua is instructed to divide the remaining land among the tribes (verse 6), indicating the distribution of land is a priority.

questions.text: Which tribe is assigned the land east of the Jordan River?
questions.explanation: Reuben is among the tribes assigned land east of the Jordan (verse 15).

questions.text: What is the status of the land of the Philistines according to Joshua 13?
options: It is fully assigned to Judah
questions.explanation: The Philistine territory is listed among the lands still remaining to be conquered (verse 2), indicating it was not yet under Israelite control.

questions.text: How many tribes are mentioned as having land allocated to them in Joshua 13?
questions.explanation: Several tribes are mentioned with assigned land, including Reuben, Gad, Manasseh, Judah, and others, totaling at least nine tribes in the distribution (verses 8–33).

questions.text: What is Joshua's instruction regarding the inheritance of the tribes east of the Jordan?
options: Assign land as commanded by Moses
Leave it to the tribes to decide
questions.explanation: Joshua is to allocate the land to those tribes as Moses had instructed, ensuring proper inheritance (verse 8).

questions.text: Which tribe's land is specifically listed starting from 'Reuben' and ending with 'Gad' in Joshua 13?
questions.explanation: The passage provides details about the land inheritance for Reuben and Gad (verse 15–23).

questions.text: What remains to be done regarding the land territories at the time of Joshua 13?
questions.explanation: The chapter indicates that the remaining land, including territories of the Philistines and others, has yet to be conquered (verse 2).

questions.text: How old was Caleb when he received his inheritance?
questions.explanation: Caleb was 85 years old when he received Hebron as his inheritance, as stated in Joshua 14:10-11.

questions.text: What was Caleb's request regarding the land of Hebron?
questions.explanation: Caleb requested to possess the land of Hebron, which he claimed was promised to him by God (Joshua 14:12).

questions.text: How did the Lord respond to Caleb’s request?
questions.explanation: The Lord granted Caleb’s request and gave him the land he desired (Joshua 14:14).

questions.text: What was Caleb's attitude towards the strength of the land's inhabitants?
questions.explanation: Caleb expressed confidence in conquering the land, stating the Lord would give it into their hands (Joshua 14:12).

questions.text: What does Caleb emphasize about himself at this age?
questions.explanation: Caleb mentions that he is still strong and able to go out and come in even at 85, highlighting his enduring strength (Joshua 14:11).

questions.text: Which city did Caleb request to inherit?
questions.explanation: Caleb requested Hebron, which was part of the land allocated to him and his descendants (Joshua 14:13).

questions.text: In what way does Caleb's story serve as an example for believers?
options: To trust God's promises and remain faithful
questions.explanation: Caleb's confidence in God's promises and his faithfulness serve as an example for believers to trust God's word at any age (Joshua 14).

questions.text: Which city’s boundary is described in Joshua 15:1?
questions.explanation: Joshua 15:1 begins with the allotment for the tribe of Judah, describing its boundary from the wilderness of Zin to the south.

questions.text: In Joshua 15, which is the significant city allocated to Judah?
questions.explanation: Joshua 15:13 mentions that Caleb received Hebron as part of his inheritance, which was within the territory assigned to Judah.

questions.text: What is the reason given in Joshua 15:8 for the city of Zorah’s location?
questions.explanation: Joshua 15:8 describes Zorah as being between two valleys, specifying its geographical position.

questions.text: Which tribe is allocated the city of Beersheba in Joshua 15?
questions.explanation: Joshua 15:21 specifically lists Beersheba as part of Judah's inheritance.

questions.text: Which prominent figure is associated with Hebron in Joshua 15?
questions.explanation: Joshua 15:13-14 notes Caleb received Hebron as his inheritance, highlighting his significance in this chapter.

questions.text: What theme is primarily illustrated in Joshua 15 regarding Judah’s inheritance?
questions.explanation: The chapter details the boundaries and cities given to Judah, reflecting themes of conquest and land allocation.

questions.text: How many cities are listed within Judah’s inheritance in Joshua 15?
questions.explanation: In Joshua 15:20-63, many cities are listed, with the total number of distinct city names reaching sixteen.

questions.text: What is the significance of the boundary descriptions in Joshua 15?
questions.explanation: The boundary descriptions serve to define the land allocated to each tribe, specifically Judah in this chapter.

questions.text: Which tribe's territory is described in Joshua 16?
questions.explanation: Joshua 16 details the territory allocated to the tribe of Benjamin and part of Ephraim's territory. This chapter specifies their boundaries and settlements (verses 1-10).

questions.text: What is notable about the allocation of land in Joshua 16?
options: It was given entirely to Ephraim
It was divided among multiple tribes
It was assigned to the Levites
questions.explanation: Joshua 16 describes the division of land primarily between the tribes of Ephraim and Benjamin, indicating the process of allotting territory among the tribes (verses 1-10).

questions.text: According to Joshua 16, how are the boundaries of Benjamin's territory described?
options: From the Jordan to the sea
From the river to the border of Judah
questions.explanation: The boundaries of Benjamin's territory include areas from the Jordan River to the border with Judah, as described in verses 5-9 of Joshua 16.

questions.text: What cities are included within the territory of Benjamin as per Joshua 16?
questions.explanation: The chapter mentions cities such as Jerusalem and Bethel within Benjamin's territory (verse 10).

questions.text: How is the assignment of land to the tribes of Ephraim and Benjamin described in Joshua 16?
options: It was organized by the leaders of each tribe
It was decided through a divine vision
questions.explanation: The chapter indicates that the land was divided among the tribal leaders under Joshua's supervision, following God's instructions (verse 4).

questions.text: What does Joshua 16 indicate about the completeness of the land allocation?
options: All land was assigned to Ephraim
The land was assigned to all tribes except Levi
Most of the land was still unclaimed
questions.explanation: The chapter shows that the land was allocated to tribes, but Levites did not receive territorial allotments as their portion was different (implied from verse 10).

questions.text: What is the significance of the area named in Joshua 16 for the tribes involved?
options: It became the capital of Israel
It was a central portion for Benjamin and Ephraim
questions.explanation: The designated area was central to the territories of Benjamin and Ephraim, important tribal regions within the land distribution (verses 5-10).

questions.text: What was the purpose of Joshua 16 in the context of Israel's conquest?
options: To recount the allocation of territory
To record the building of shrines
questions.explanation: Joshua 16 records the territorial boundaries assigned to the tribes of Ephraim and Benjamin, part of the broader land division following conquest.

questions.text: Which tribe's territory is described as having great and numerous people in Joshua 17?
questions.explanation: Joshua 17 describes the descendants of Joseph, specifically mentioning their numerous people and land. Joseph's line includes Manasseh and Ephraim, but the chapter focuses on Joseph's allocation.

questions.text: What did the descendants of Manasseh request from Joshua?
questions.explanation: The descendants of Manasseh asked for cities to settle in, as described in Joshua 17:11-12, because their land was not fully conquered yet.

questions.text: How did Joshua respond to the request for more land from Manasseh?
options: He encouraged them to clear remaining forests
He assigned them neighboring tribes' land
questions.explanation: Joshua advised that they clear the wooded areas of the land they had, indicating they had to work to possess the land they request (Joshua 17:15).

questions.text: Which tribes' land was described as being divided among the descendants of Joseph?
questions.explanation: The chapter discusses the land allocated to the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, both descendants of Joseph.

questions.text: What geographical feature is mentioned as a challenge for the tribe of Manasseh in conquering land?
questions.explanation: The chapter mentions the difficult terrain of the forests and wooded areas that the tribe of Manasseh needed to clear to possess their land (Joshua 17:15).

questions.text: What attitude is shown by Joshua towards the tribes' requests for land?
options: He encourages them to be brave and work
questions.explanation: Joshua acknowledges their needs and encourages them to work to clear the land they have, showing an optimistic and proactive attitude (Joshua 17:15).

questions.text: Which tribe's territory is explicitly described as not being fully settled or possessed in Joshua 17?
questions.explanation: The descendants of Manasseh faced difficulties in fully possessing their territory, prompting their request for more land, as described in Joshua 17.

questions.text: What was the main reason the descendants of Manasseh wanted more land?
options: Their territory had forests to clear
They had not received their full allotment
questions.explanation: The chapter indicates that the descendants of Manasseh believed they had not yet received their full allotment of land and asked for more (Joshua 17:14).

questions.text: What did Joshua do to prepare the land after settling the tribes?
questions.explanation: Joshua 18:1 states that the land had not yet been divided among the tribes, implying the need to do so; the chapter describes how they set up to finalize this process, including dividing the land into lots.

questions.text: How many tribes had not yet received their inheritance at the beginning of Joshua 18?
questions.explanation: Joshua 18:2 indicates that seven tribes still had not received their inheritance, prompting Joshua to instruct them to prepare to cast lots.

questions.text: What did the Levites receive as their inheritance?
questions.explanation: Joshua 18:7 states that the Levites were given cities to dwell in and pasturelands around them, rather than a large land parcel like other tribes.

questions.text: What task did the tribes undertake after receiving their assignments?
options: Made a covenant with neighboring nations
questions.explanation: Joshua 18:6 and 8 describe how the tribes prepared to cast lots in order to determine their specific land allocations, after receiving their instructions.

questions.text: How did Joshua instruct the tribes regarding their land divisions?
questions.explanation: Joshua 18:4-6 reveals that Joshua advised the tribes to prepare and cast lots to determine their inheritance, trusting God's guidance in the process.

questions.text: Which city was among the land divisions mentioned in Joshua 18?
questions.explanation: Joshua 18 references Gibeon as one of the towns included in the land allotments for the tribes, specifically mentioned in verse 25.

questions.text: What was the significance of the division of the land among the tribes?
options: It established territorial boundaries for justice
It fulfilled God's promise to Israel
It allowed tribes to establish independent nations
It replaced the previous land distribution system
questions.explanation: The division of land in Joshua 18 fulfilled God's promise to give Israel the land, making it an important step in their inheritance and settling in the Promised Land.

questions.text: Which tribe's allotment is described first in Joshua 19?
questions.explanation: The chapter begins with the allotment for the tribe of Asher in Joshua 19:24-31.

questions.text: How many cities did the tribe of Naphtali receive in their allotment?
questions.explanation: Naphtali's territory included seven cities, as listed in Joshua 19:32-39.

questions.text: Which tribe's land included the city of Jezreel?
questions.explanation: Jezreel was part of the land assigned to the tribe of Manasseh, as outlined in Joshua 19:17-23.

questions.text: What is a notable feature of the allotments described in Joshua 19?
options: They included cities and rural areas
questions.explanation: The allotments included both cities and surrounding rural areas for each tribe, as detailed throughout the chapter.

questions.text: Which tribe received the largest territory in Joshua 19?
questions.explanation: Asher's allotment was notably extensive, covering a significant area along the coast as described in Joshua 19:24-31.

questions.text: Who assigned the land to the tribes in Joshua 19?
questions.explanation: Joshua is documented as the one overseeing the allotments for the tribes as shown in verses 1 and 50.

questions.text: Are any of the tribe allotments described as incomplete in Joshua 19?
options: Only the southern regions are incomplete
questions.explanation: The chapter provides a complete list of the tribe allotments; there is no mention of incomplete descriptions.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of Joshua 19?
options: To record the division of land among the tribes
questions.explanation: Joshua 19 details how the land was allotted to each tribe, serving as a record of the division of the land.

questions.text: Where do the spies hide in Joshua 2?
questions.explanation: The spies hide in Rahab's house on the wall, as described in Joshua 2:15.

questions.text: What request does Rahab make to the spies when they meet her?
options: To find out about the city
questions.explanation: Rahab requests the spies to spare her and her family when they deliver Jericho's destruction, as stated in Joshua 2:12-13.

questions.text: What do the spies instruct Rahab to do to ensure her safety?
options: Tie a scarlet cord in the window
questions.explanation: The spies tell Rahab to tie a scarlet cord in the window as a sign for her safety, according to Joshua 2:18.

questions.text: What is Rahab's profession mentioned in Joshua 2?
questions.explanation: Rahab is described as a prostitute, which is significant in her story and her faith, as seen in Joshua 2:1.

questions.text: How do the spies leave Jericho after visiting Rahab?
questions.explanation: The spies escape by climbing out through the window tied with the scarlet cord and hiding in the mountains, as described in Joshua 2:15-16.

questions.text: What is the main reason Rahab shows kindness to the spies?
options: She wants to join their camp
questions.explanation: Rahab recognizes the power of the Israelites' God and shows kindness out of faith and fear of Him, as implied in Joshua 2:9-11.

questions.text: What strategic advantage does the scarlet cord symbolize in Rahab's house?
questions.explanation: The scarlet cord serves as a sign of protection and salvation for Rahab and her family, indicating they will be spared, as in Joshua 2:18.

questions.text: What trust do the spies show in Rahab's house?
options: They trust her to protect them
They trust her to betray Jericho
They trust her to hide their weapons
They trust her to deliver a message
questions.explanation: The spies trust Rahab to safeguard them and to keep her promise of loyalty, especially through the cord and her hiding of them in Joshua 2:8-14.

questions.text: What is the primary purpose of Joshua 20?
options: To list the tribes of Israel
questions.explanation: Joshua 20 primarily instructs the Israelites about the cities of refuge where individuals can find protection from revenge (verse 2).

questions.text: How many cities of refuge are commanded to be set up?
questions.explanation: The chapter specifies that there should be seven cities of refuge across the land (verse 7).

questions.text: Who is allowed to flee to the cities of refuge?
questions.explanation: The cities are specifically designated for someone who has committed manslaughter, seeking refuge from revenge (verse 3).

questions.text: What is the role of the congregation in functions related to the cities of refuge?
options: They uphold justice and hold the trial
questions.explanation: The congregation is involved in the justice process, ensuring fair trial and protection for those fleeing to the refuge cities (verse 4).

questions.text: What must someone do before entering a city of refuge?
options: Make a sacrifice at the city gate
questions.explanation: The individual fleeing must seek refuge promptly and without delay, to avoid retribution (verse 3).

questions.text: What happens if someone leaves a city of refuge after administering justice?
options: They may be harmed by the avenger
questions.explanation: Leaving the city of refuge exposed the person to retribution from the avenger of blood, as per God’s law (implied in the chapter).

questions.text: Who appointed the cities of refuge according to Joshua 20?
options: Moses and Joshua under God's command
questions.explanation: God instructs Joshua to set up the cities of refuge, following the command given through Moses (verse 1, implied).

questions.text: What is the enduring significance of the cities of refuge in Israel’s justice system?
options: They ensure compassionate justice for manslaughter
questions.explanation: The cities of refuge provided a fair and merciful way to handle manslaughter cases, preventing revenge cycles and ensuring justice (overall theme of Joshua 20).

questions.text: What did the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh do after crossing Jordan?
options: Built an altar on the east side
Set up an altar in the Promised Land
questions.explanation: They built an altar on the east side of the Jordan as a sign of unity and faith (Joshua 22:10).

questions.text: Why did the other Israelite tribes become concerned about the altar built by Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh?
options: They thought it was for offering sacrifices
They feared it was meant for ritual worship outside the proper place
They believed it was a sign of rebellion
They wanted to take it down
questions.explanation: They feared the altar was a form of ritualism that could lead Israel away from proper worship at the sanctuary (Joshua 22:11-12).

questions.text: How did Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh clarify their purpose for building the altar?
options: They intended to use it for sacrifices
It was a memorial and witness among the tribes
It was for worship of other gods
They planned to offer sacrifices in secret
questions.explanation: They explained the altar was a witness to future generations that they too are Israelites and part of God's covenant (Joshua 22:26-27).

questions.text: What was the primary concern expressed by the other tribes regarding the altar?
options: That it was not built at the sanctuary
That it was used for offerings
questions.explanation: Their concern was that the altar might appear as a rival place of worship, which could threaten the unity of Israel (Joshua 22:11-12).

questions.text: How did Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh respond to the concerns about the altar?
options: They explained its purpose as symbolic
They insisted it was for sacrifices
questions.explanation: They explained that the altar was built as a witness to future generations of their connection to Israel and God's covenant (Joshua 22:26-27).

questions.text: What action did the other tribes take after hearing the explanation about the altar?
options: They sent messengers to confirm their intentions
questions.explanation: They sent to confirm the intentions of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, seeking understanding before taking further action (Joshua 22:13-15).

questions.text: What was Joshua’s instruction to the tribes regarding the altar’s purpose?
options: To build their own altars elsewhere
To act in peace and confirm their identity as Israelites
questions.explanation: Joshua told them to be at peace and assured them that the altar was a witness to their shared identity as God's people (Joshua 22:20-21).

questions.text: What lesson can we learn from the response of the tribes regarding the altar?
questions.explanation: The tribes’ willingness to clarify and communicate shows the importance of understanding and dialogue in resolving concerns (Joshua 22).

questions.text: What did Joshua instruct the people to do as he prepared to leave them?
questions.explanation: Joshua 23:6 emphasizes that Joshua urged the people to be careful to love the Lord and serve Him faithfully.

questions.text: According to Joshua 23, what was Joshua's final call to Israel?
options: To adhere to the law of Moses
To serve the Lord with all their heart and soul
To leave Canaan and return to their homes
questions.explanation: Joshua 23:11-14 emphasizes his final exhortation for Israelites to love and serve the Lord wholeheartedly.

questions.text: What warning does Joshua give regarding the nations remaining in the land?
options: They will become allies if respected
They might become a snare or trap
questions.explanation: Joshua 23:13 warns that the remaining nations will be a snare or trap if Israelites intermarry or turn away from God.

questions.text: How did Joshua describe his own life at this point in Joshua 23?
options: An old and advanced age with many years
questions.explanation: Joshua 23:14 states that Joshua is 'old and advanced in age,' marking his nearing end of life.

questions.text: What is Joshua's main encouragement to Israel about God's promises?
options: God has been faithful to all His promises
questions.explanation: Joshua 23:14 emphasizes that all God's promises to Israel have been fulfilled, encouraging trust in His faithfulness.

questions.text: What act does Joshua threaten to do if Israel turns away from the Lord?
questions.explanation: Joshua 23:16 warns that turning away from the Lord brings consequences, including disinheritance and calamity, as the Lord will no longer continue to drive out their enemies.

questions.text: According to Joshua 23, what is the importance of obeying the Law of Moses?
options: It is essential to remain committed to God
It is a ceremonial act only
It is irrelevant in the new land
questions.explanation: Joshua 23:6 highlights the importance of faithfully obeying God's law as a sign of love and commitment to the Lord.

questions.text: What does Joshua say about himself in Joshua 23:14?
options: He is ready to lead again
questions.explanation: Joshua 23:14 states that Joshua is old and near death, emphasizing the nearing end of his leadership and life.

questions.text: What did Joshua do at Shechem in Joshua 24?
options: He built an altar to the Lord
He gathered all tribes for a covenant renewal
He led a prayer service at the temple
questions.explanation: In Joshua 24:1, Joshua gathers all tribes at Shechem to renew the covenant with God. This act signifies a formal recommitment to serve the Lord.

questions.text: What did Joshua challenge the people to do in Joshua 24:15?
options: Decide to serve the gods of their ancestors
questions.explanation: Joshua 24:15 includes his famous declaration, 'Choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve,' urging the people to make a decisive commitment.

questions.text: How does Joshua describe what the Lord did for Israel in Joshua 24?
options: He brought them out of Egypt
He made a covenant with Abraham
He fought for them and gave them land
questions.explanation: In Joshua 24:12, Joshua recounts how God fought for Israel, driving out nations and giving them the land, illustrating God's active assistance.

questions.text: What did the people respond to Joshua's challenge in Joshua 24?
options: They promised to serve the Lord
They chose to serve the gods of their ancestors
They asked for more time to decide
questions.explanation: In Joshua 24:24, the people publicly reaffirm their commitment to serve the Lord, confirming their decision to follow Him.

questions.text: What did Joshua do after the people committed to serve the Lord?
options: He built an altar of stones
He wrote a covenant in the Book of the Law
questions.explanation: Joshua 24:26 states that he took a large stone and set it up under the oak near the sanctuary, symbolizing the covenant and its documentation.

questions.text: What was Joshua’s final act in Joshua 24?
options: He defended the land from enemies
He established a new religious feast
questions.explanation: Joshua 24:29 states that Joshua died at the age of 110 and was buried in the land of his inheritance, marking the end of his leadership.

questions.text: How long did Joshua serve as leader of Israel according to Joshua 24?
questions.explanation: Joshua 24:29 mentions that he served as leader until his death at age 110, indicating a long period of leadership over Israel.

questions.text: Where did the Israelites camp before crossing the Jordan River?
questions.explanation: In Joshua 3:1, the Israelites camped at the place called Gilgal before crossing the Jordan River.

questions.text: What did Joshua instruct the people to do when they saw the priests carrying the Ark of the Covenant?
questions.explanation: Joshua 3:3-4 instructs the Israelites to follow the priests carrying the Ark, keeping a distance so they can see the way as they follow the Ark into the Jordan.

questions.text: What was the significance of the Ark of the Covenant in this chapter?
questions.explanation: The Ark of the Covenant symbolized God's presence among the Israelites, as emphasized throughout Joshua 3 when it is carried ahead of the people into the rushing Jordan.

questions.text: What did the priests do when their feet dipped into the Jordan River?
questions.explanation: According to Joshua 3:15-16, when the priests' feet touched the water, the flow of the Jordan River stopped, allowing the people to cross on dry ground.

questions.text: How did the people know it was safe to cross the Jordan?
options: The priests stood in the river
The priests' feet touched the water and it stopped flowing
questions.explanation: Joshua 3:17 explains that the priests standing with the Ark in the middle of the Jordan caused the water to stop flowing, making it safe for the people to cross.

questions.text: What was Joshua’s command after crossing the Jordan?
questions.explanation: Joshua 4:1-3 records Joshua's instruction to set up memorial stones as a lasting reminder of God's miracle in stopping the Jordan's waters.

questions.text: What purpose did the memorial stones serve?
questions.explanation: The memorial stones served as a reminder to future generations of the miraculous crossing and God's faithfulness, as explained in Joshua 4:7.

questions.text: What did the Israelites do with the 12 stones they took from the Jordan River?
options: Used them for a new altar
Cast them into the river again
questions.explanation: The Israelites set up 12 stones at Gilgal as a memorial to remind them of God's miracle in crossing the Jordan (verses 3-7).

questions.text: Why did Joshua command the Israelites to choose 12 men, one from each tribe?
options: To carry the stones out of the river
To set up a memorial at Gilgal
To bring offerings to the Lord
questions.explanation: Joshua instructed one man from each tribe to take a stone from the Jordan to build a monument at Gilgal as a lasting memorial (verses 2-3, 6-7).

questions.text: What does the crossing of the Jordan symbolize for the Israelites?
options: A test of their faith with no lasting significance
questions.explanation: The crossing symbolizes God's faithfulness in leading His people into the land and marks a new beginning, as they enter the Promised Land (verses 1-7).

questions.text: How did the Israelites know that the Lord had dried up the Jordan River?
options: By seeing the water pile up upstream
Because they heard a loud roar
questions.explanation: The water stopped flowing and piled up upstream, allowing Israel to cross on dry ground (verse 23).

questions.text: What specific instruction did God give the priests carrying the Ark of the Covenant?
options: Stand firm in the middle of the river
Keep walking into the river until told otherwise
Set up an altar on the riverbank
questions.explanation: God told the priests to keep walking into the Jordan until all the people had crossed (verses 8-9).

questions.text: What is the significance of the stones taken from the Jordan River?
options: They were used to build the walls of Jericho
They serve as a reminder of God's mighty act
They were stored for future sacrifices
They were thrown into the wilderness
questions.explanation: The stones serve as a lasting memorial to remind future generations of God's miraculous intervention (verses 6-7).

questions.text: Who led the Israelites across the Jordan River?
questions.explanation: Joshua was the leader who led the Israelites across the Jordan into the Promised Land (verses 1-2).

questions.text: What did Joshua command the people to do after crossing the Jordan?
options: Celebrate with a feast and set up memorial stones
questions.explanation: Joshua commanded the people to celebrate, keep the memorial stones, and remember God's miracle (verse 19-24).

questions.text: What did the Israelites do after crossing the Jordan River according to Joshua 5?
options: Set up a memorial at Gilgal
questions.explanation: In Joshua 5:2-3, the Israelites were circumcised at Gilgal, signifying the renewal of their covenant with God after crossing the Jordan.

questions.text: Why did the Israelites celebrate Passover in Joshua 5?
options: To commemorate their deliverance from Egypt
To honor God's provision in the wilderness
Because it was a tradition before battle
questions.explanation: Joshua 5:10-11 states that they celebrated Passover to remember God's deliverance from Egypt and their journey to the Promised Land.

questions.text: What did the commander of the Lord’s army tell Joshua in Joshua 5?
questions.explanation: In Joshua 5:15, the commander instructs Joshua to remove his sandals because he is standing on holy ground, echoing God's command to Moses in Exodus.

questions.text: What symbol was used to mark the Israelites’ completion of their circumcisions?
questions.explanation: While not explicitly stated as a symbol, the Passover celebration in Joshua 5 signifies their new identity and covenant with God after circumcision, which was a sign of the covenant.

questions.text: How many days did the Israelites remain in their camp at Gilgal after crossing the Jordan?
questions.explanation: Joshua 5:10-11 indicates they kept the Passover and celebrated there, which took place shortly after crossing the Jordan, typically understood as a week-long period of observation.

questions.text: What miraculous event occurred related to the manna in Joshua 5?
questions.explanation: Joshua 5:12 states that after they ate the produce of Canaan, manna ceased, signaling the end of God's provision of manna in the wilderness.

questions.text: What is the significance of the name 'Gilgal' where the Israelites camped?
questions.explanation: Joshua 5:9 indicates that Gilgal means 'circle' or 'wheel,' symbolizing God's rolling away the disgrace of Egypt and marking a new start for Israel.

questions.text: What was Joshua’s response after seeing the commander of the Lord’s army?
questions.explanation: In Joshua 5:14, Joshua fell facedown in worship when he saw the commander, recognizing God's presence and authority.

questions.text: What did the Israelites do when they encircled Jericho according to Joshua 6?
options: They shouted loudly and blew trumpets
They fought the city walls directly
They climbed over the walls covertly
questions.explanation: In Joshua 6:20, the Israelites shouted and blew trumpets after circling Jericho, causing the walls to fall. This was part of God's instructions for defeating the city.

questions.text: What specific instructions did Joshua receive from the Lord for conquering Jericho?
options: Attack with all soldiers at once
March around the city once for six days, then seven times on the seventh day
Lay siege for a month before attacking
questions.explanation: Joshua 6:3-4 details God's command to march around Jericho once per day for six days, and seven times on the seventh day, with priests blowing horns before the walls fell.

questions.text: What did the people do after the walls of Jericho fell?
options: They entered and took the city
They continued marching around the city
They set up an altar outside the city
questions.explanation: Joshua 6:20 states that the people entered the city and destroyed it after the walls fell, following God's command.

questions.text: What was the fate of Rahab and her family in Jericho?
options: They were spared and kept alive
They escaped before the walls fell
They hid inside the city walls
questions.explanation: Joshua 6:22-23 notes that Rahab and her family were spared and kept alive because she hid the spies and helped Israel.

questions.text: What act of disobedience led to the defeat at Ai that is mentioned earlier in Joshua?
options: Achan took items devoted to destruction
They did not blow the trumpets
They entered Jericho before God's instruction
questions.explanation: Earlier in Joshua (not in chapter 6 but relevant context), Achan's sin in taking items from Jericho led to Israel's defeat at Ai, showing the importance of obedience.

questions.text: How did the Israelites ensure the city walls fell during the march around Jericho?
options: By shouting loudly and blowing trumpets
By setting off an early earthquake
By closing the city gates from outside
questions.explanation: In Joshua 6:20, the Israelites' shouts and trumpet blasts accompanied by their marching caused the walls to collapse, according to God's plan.

questions.text: What was one reason that the walls of Jericho fell?
options: Because God's power caused them to collapse
Due to an earthquake caused by the Israelites
Because the city abandoned its defenses
Because of enemy fire from neighboring cities
questions.explanation: Joshua 6 emphasizes that the walls fell because of God's power, as He gave Israel victory through their obedience to His instructions.

questions.text: What was the main lesson from the victory at Jericho?
options: Obedience to God's commands brings victory
Walls are easily defeated with trumpets
questions.explanation: The story highlights that obedience to God's specific instructions was key to victory, demonstrating faith and trust in His power.

questions.text: Who was the man who secretly took some of the devoted things?
questions.explanation: Achan is identified in Joshua 7:1 as the man who took some of the devoted things after the fall of Jericho, which led to Israel's defeat at Ai.

questions.text: What was the consequence of Israel's defeat at Ai?
questions.explanation: The defeat was due to Israel's disobedience, specifically Achan's sin, which caused God's displeasure as explained in Joshua 7:1-2 and following verses.

questions.text: How did Joshua respond when Israel was defeated at Ai?
options: He fell facedown before the Ark
He sent spies to gather information
questions.explanation: Joshua’s initial response was to fall facedown and seek God's guidance, as described in Joshua 7:6-7.

questions.text: What instruction does Joshua give the people before the attack on Ai in Joshua 8?
options: To set an ambush behind the city
questions.explanation: Joshua instructs the people to set an ambush behind the city (verse 2), which is crucial for their tactical plan.

questions.text: What does Joshua tell the soldiers to do when attacking Ai the second time?
options: Lure the city with a small force and ambush behind
Surround the city silently at night
questions.explanation: Joshua commands the main force to pretend to retreat while the ambush forces surprise Ai from behind (verse 2-3).

questions.text: What is the purpose of the ambush in Joshua 8?
options: To set fire to the city
To lure the king into a trap
To cause confusion and capture the city
To test the strength of Ai's defenses
questions.explanation: The ambush aims to cause confusion among the inhabitants, leading to their defeat and the city's capture (verse 2).

questions.text: How do the Israelites approach Ai before the attack as described in Joshua 8?
options: They march directly into the city
They circle around the city repeatedly
They set an ambush behind the city
They call out to the inhabitants peacefully
questions.explanation: Joshua orders the ambush behind Ai, preparing for a surprise attack (verse 2).

questions.text: What sign indicates to the Israelites that their plan to attack Ai has succeeded?
options: The smoke from the city rises high
The city gates are broken down
They see the sun shining on the walls
The king of Ai is captured
questions.explanation: The smoke rising from Ai signals the fire set by the ambush, confirming the victory (verse 18).

questions.text: What does Joshua do after capturing Ai?
options: He destroys the city and its inhabitants
He repopulates the city with new settlers
He negotiates a treaty with Ai’s king
questions.explanation: Joshua destroys Ai and its inhabitants, following God's command (verse 26-28).

questions.text: Why does Joshua make a memorial at Mount Ebal after the victory?
options: To set up an idol for worship
To reaffirm the covenant with God
To mark the spot of their victory
questions.explanation: Joshua builds an altar to renew the covenant with God, emphasizing obedience and God's promises (verses 30-31).

questions.text: What instructions are given regarding the words written on the stones at Mount Ebal?
options: To read them annually to all Israelites
questions.explanation: The chapter emphasizes the importance of reading the instructions and covenant written on the stones to all Israelites (verse 34).

questions.text: What strategy did the Gibeonites use to make peace with Israel according to Joshua 9?
options: They pretended to be from a distant land
questions.explanation: The Gibeonites resorted to deception by pretending to be travelers from a distant land (Joshua 9:4-5).

questions.text: How did the Israelites discover the Gibeonites’ deception?
options: They found evidence in the city records
They overheard the Gibeonites speaking nearby
They discovered their clothing and food supplies
questions.explanation: The Israelites examined the Gibeonites' provisions and clothing, realizing they had lied about their origins (Joshua 9:14-15).

questions.text: What was the Israelites’ initial reaction upon learning the Gibeonites’ deception?
options: They immediately appointed them as allies
They dishonored their oath and fought them
They honored their oath and spared them
They expelled them from the land
questions.explanation: The Israelites chose to honor their oath and did not attack the Gibeonites after discovering the deception (Joshua 9:19).

questions.text: What did the Gibeonites request from the leaders of Israel?
options: They wanted to become part of Israel
questions.explanation: The Gibeonites asked for protection and peace, which the leaders of Israel granted (Joshua 9:15).

questions.text: Why was the deception of the Gibeonites considered a serious matter?
options: It led to a war among tribes
It violated the covenant with God
It tricked Israel into making an oath
It caused the king of Gibeon to be king
questions.explanation: Their deception led Israel to swear an oath to spare them, which they felt bound to honor (Joshua 9:15-20).

questions.text: What did the Israelites do with the Gibeonites after discovering their deception?
options: They expelled them from the land
They kept their promise and spared them
questions.explanation: Despite the deception, the Israelites honored their oath and allowed the Gibeonites to live among them (Joshua 9:21).

questions.text: What is a key lesson from the Gibeonites' story in Joshua 9?
options: Deception is acceptable when it benefits peace
Honoring promises is important, even when dealing with deception
All alliances in warfare should be avoided
questions.explanation: The story highlights the importance of keeping promises and integrity, even when others deceive (Joshua 9).

questions.text: Who is Jude in relation to Jesus?
questions.explanation: Jude identifies himself as 'a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James,' indicating his familial relation to Jesus. This is stated in Jude 1:1.

questions.text: To whom is Jude writing his letter?
options: To those loved by God and kept for Jesus Christ
questions.explanation: Jude addresses his recipients as 'those who are called, loved by God the Father, and kept for Jesus Christ,' emphasizing their spiritual relationship with God. This is found in Jude 1:1.

questions.text: What does Jude call certain individuals who infiltrate the church?
questions.explanation: Jude describes these individuals as 'certain people who have secretly slipped in,' labeling them as 'ungodly' and causing trouble within the church. This is in Jude 1:4.

questions.text: What reason does Jude give for warning the believers about these certain infiltrators?
options: They turn others away from the faith
questions.explanation: Jude warns that these individuals 'turn others' every which way, leading them away from the faith,' which threatens the spiritual well-being of believers, as stated in Jude 1:4.

questions.text: What examples from the past does Jude mention to warn about God's judgment?
options: The flood during Noah's time and Sodom and Gomorrah
The fall of Lucifer and the destruction of Jerusalem
The rebellion of Korah and Pharaoh's plagues
The giants in Canaan and the exile of Israel
questions.explanation: Jude references the destruction of the ungodly in Noah's time and the punishment of Sodom and Gomorrah as examples of divine judgment, found in Jude 1:6-7.

questions.text: What comparison does Jude make to describe the false teachers?
questions.explanation: Jude describes these corrupters as 'hidden reefs at your love feasts,' symbolizing danger and causing shipwreck of faith, as in Jude 1:12.

questions.text: What is Jude's main plea to the believers at the beginning of his letter?
questions.explanation: Jude urges believers to 'contend earnestly for the faith that was once for all entrusted to God's holy people,' emphasizing the importance of steadfastness in faith (Jude 1:3).

questions.text: What did the Israelites ask the Lord at the beginning of Judges 1?
options: Who will lead us in battle?
Who shall go up first for us?
How can we defeat our enemies?
questions.explanation: In Judges 1:1, the Israelites inquired of the Lord, asking 'Who shall go up first for us?' indicating their seeking guidance for military action.

questions.text: Which tribe was assigned to take Jerusalem according to Judges 1?
questions.explanation: Judah was the tribe that succeeded in capturing Jerusalem, as mentioned in Judges 1:8, where they defeated the inhabitants and set the city on fire.

questions.text: Which tribe failed to drive out the Canaanites from their territory?
questions.explanation: Judges 1:19 states that the tribe of Ephraim failed to drive out the Canaanites and settled among them, revealing incomplete conquest.

questions.text: What notable victory did the tribe of Judah achieve in Judges 1?
options: Drove out the Canaanites from Hebron
questions.explanation: Judges 1:20 mentions that Judah successfully took Hebron, driving out the three sons of Anak as part of their victory.

questions.text: What is said about the tribes of Benjamin and Joseph in Judges 1?
options: They were unable to conquer their territories
They partially drove out the inhabitants
They did not attempt to fight
questions.explanation: Judges 1:21 states that the tribes of Benjamin and Joseph did not fully drive out the Canaanites and lived among them, leading to ongoing conflicts.

questions.text: What does Judges 1 indicate about the overall success of the Israelites in conquering the land?
options: They had partial success, leaving some Canaanites in the land
They conquered all enemies without resistance
They immediately received victory from God
questions.explanation: Throughout Judges 1, it is clear that the Israelites experienced partial success; they conquered some areas but left others unconquered, which is highlighted in their incomplete conquest efforts.

questions.text: Which tribe was excluded from fighting at times according to Judges 1?
questions.explanation: Judges 1 mentions that Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites from their territories and instead made peace with some, implying incomplete obedience.

questions.text: What pattern emerges regarding the Israelites' conquest in Judges 1?
options: A pattern of partial victories and compromises
questions.explanation: Judges 1 reveals a pattern where Israel had some victories but often did not fully conquer or drive out the inhabitants, leading to ongoing struggles.

questions.text: Who was Tola in Judges 10?
options: A judge who judged Israel for 23 years
questions.explanation: Tola is described as a judge who judged Israel for 23 years, providing leadership and stability during that period (Judges 10:1-2).

questions.text: What was Jair known for in Judges 10?
questions.explanation: Jair was a judge who served over Israel for 22 years, as mentioned in Judges 10:3-5, providing leadership during his time.

questions.text: How did the Israelites respond to their distress in Judges 10?
options: They sought help from neighboring nations
They cried out to the Lord
questions.explanation: The Israelites cried out to the Lord because they were suffering under Midian and other oppressions, prompting God's response (Judges 10:10).

questions.text: How did God react when Israel cried out to Him in Judges 10?
questions.explanation: God responded to Israel’s cry by raising up judges to deliver them, showing His mercy and patience (Judges 10:11-12).

questions.text: Which nations oppressed Israel before they cried out in Judges 10?
questions.explanation: Israel was oppressed by various nations including the Midianites, Amalekites, and other groups, as described in Judges 10:7-8.

questions.text: What does Judges 10 reveal about Israel's pattern of behavior?
options: They repeatedly turned away from God and faced oppression
They only called out to God during peace
questions.explanation: Israel repeatedly fell into sin, turned away from God, faced oppression, and then cried out for help, illustrating a cyclical pattern (Judges 10:6-7).

questions.text: Why does Judges 10 emphasize the lengths to which Israel's judges went to deliver the people?
options: To highlight God's mercy and patience
questions.explanation: The chapter emphasizes God's mercy and patience in raising judges despite Israel’s repeated disobedience and turning away from Him (Judges 10:13-14).

questions.text: What is the overall message of Judges 10 about Israel's relationship with God?
options: They continually stray and need God's mercy
They succeed through their own strength
questions.explanation: Judges 10 highlights the cycle of Israel's disobedience, their cries for help, and God's mercy in raising deliverers, underscoring their dependence on God's grace.

questions.text: Who was the leader of the tribe of Benjamin in Judges 11?
questions.explanation: Jephthah was the GTJI leader of the tribe of Benjamin who led Israel in Judges 11 (verse 1).

questions.text: What was Jephthah known for before leading Israel?
options: Being a mighty man of valor
questions.explanation: Jephthah was described as an outcast and a warrior from Gilead, which is emphasized in verses 1-2.

questions.text: How did Jephthah respond to the elders’ request to lead the fight against the Ammonites?
questions.explanation: Jephthah accepted to lead Israel against the Ammonites after the elders asked him and promised to make him ruler, as described in verses 4-11.

questions.text: What did Jephthah do before going into battle?
questions.explanation: Jephthah prayed to the Lord and made a vow, promising if victorious, he would offer whatever comes out of his house, as seen in verse 30-31.

questions.text: What was the outcome of Jephthah’s vow?
options: His daughter came out to greet him
questions.explanation: Jephthah’s daughter came out to greet him, and he realized he had made a vow involving her, leading to a tragic outcome, described in verses 34-39.

questions.text: How did Jephthah’s story highlight the importance of what?
questions.explanation: Jephthah’s story underscores the importance of obedience to God's will, especially in vows and commitments, as discussed throughout the chapter.

questions.text: What did Jephthah do after his victory over the Ammonites?
questions.explanation: Jephthah assumed leadership and became ruler over Gilead after his victory, as indicated in verses 11 and 12.

questions.text: What lesson can we learn from Jephthah's story?
questions.explanation: The story illustrates the importance of trusting and obeying God's guidance, especially when making vows, highlighting the need for careful speech.

questions.text: Who was the leader that confronted the Gileadites after the battle?
questions.explanation: Jephthah was the leader who confronted the Gileadites after the fight, as recorded in Judges 12:1-3.

questions.text: What specific demand did the Gileadites make to Ephraimites?
questions.explanation: The Gileadites asked that the Ephraimites cross the Jordan to prove their allegiance, as described in Judges 12:5-6.

questions.text: What method was used to identify Ephraimites trying to escape?
questions.explanation: The Gileadites used a password to identify Ephraimites, which led to their capture if they failed to say it correctly, as seen in Judges 12:6.

questions.text: What was the consequence for Ephraimites who failed the password test?
questions.explanation: Ephraimites who failed the password test were killed, particularly those trying to escape across the Jordan, as indicated in Judges 12:6.

questions.text: What did Jephthah do to the leaders of Ephraim after the conflict?
questions.explanation: Jephthah executed the leaders of Ephraim who could not say the password, as described in Judges 12:6.

questions.text: What was the main reason for the conflict between Gilead and Ephraim?
questions.explanation: The conflict arose over accusations and incidents related to the control of the passage across the Jordan, and Ephraim’s attempt to assert dominance, indirectly linked to issues over captives and recognition, as seen in the chapter.

questions.text: What is a key lesson from the story in Judges 12?
questions.explanation: The chapter highlights that unresolved conflicts can lead to violence and death, emphasizing the importance of addressing disputes peacefully, as demonstrated by the violent outcome of this dispute.

questions.text: Who is the main divine messenger in Judges 13?
questions.explanation: Judges 13 describes an angel of the Lord appearing to Manoah's wife, announcing the birth of Samson (verses 3-5).

questions.text: What special instruction does the angel give regarding Samson's birth?
options: He must be a Nazarite from birth
questions.explanation: The angel instructs that Samson be a Nazarite from the womb, which includes specific vows like not cutting his hair (verses 5, 7).

questions.text: Who is barren and unable to have children in Judges 13?
questions.explanation: The passage states Manoah's wife was barren and unable to conceive until the divine visit (verse 2).

questions.text: What privilege does the angel promise Manoah's wife about her son?
options: He will save Israel from the Philistines
He will lead them into battle
